# Executive summary {.unnumbered}

The COTS Control Program uses vessel and diver time to search for crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS). Crews tow manta observers around reefs and dive designated cull sites, many holding few or no COTS. Project CCIP-BR-13 set out to make that search more efficient at the scale where crews decide, within a reef. It had two strands:

- fine-scale habitat suitability layers and rankings showing where on a reef to tow and dive first;
- a prototype metacommunity model for control strategies across reef clusters.

Every search-efficiency result below was tested on held-out data against a no-information baseline at the same effort.

**Key findings**

- **The ranking reduces searches, with larger reductions at lower retention.** Retaining 80%, 90%, 95% and 99% of dives above 0.04 CPUE required `r p0(hd("sites_searched", 0.8))`, `r p0(hd("sites_searched", 0.9))`, `r p0(hd("sites_searched"))` and `r p0(hd("sites_searched", 0.99))` of sites with habitat plus recent observations. At 95% retention, random selection required `r p0(hd("sites_searched", score = "random"))`. Annual full surveys and triggered checks could help recover missed populations, but their effort and detection success need field assessment. Lower-retention options allow more high-density dives to be missed initially.
- **The earlier ≥0.02 comparison improved on habitat alone season after season.** With the evidence model trained only on earlier seasons, the combined ranking avoided more low-density dives than habitat alone in every season from 2022, and searched fewer sites in every season from 2023.
- **Each source covers the other's gaps.**
  - Past cull records plus habitat forecast next season's problematic sites with an AUC of `r a2(fvh("combined_fixed"))`, against `r a2(fvh("habitat"))` for habitat alone.
  - History lies within reach of only `r p0(hist$fraction_with_history)` of reef cells, and `r p0(n_noev / nrow(pri))` of designated sites are on reefs with no recent visits. There, habitat supplies the first search order.
  - Habitat also points to ground outside the current search footprint, where strong manta evidence was more common than on repeat ground (`r p1(pick(eng, ground = "new ground", score = "cull", metric = "auc", col = "strong_share"))` vs `r p1(pick(eng, ground = "repeat ground", score = "cull", metric = "auc", col = "strong_share"))` of tows).
- **For manta surveillance, use habitat to guide added searches.** Habitat-only tow selection did not outperform evenly spaced thinning in the retrospective comparison. Thinning is an analytical benchmark, not a practical field route. The maps are most useful alongside recent observations and crew knowledge when identifying habitats needing additional coverage.
- **The metacommunity model reproduces historical waves and now supports exploratory control projections.** Updated simulations compare COTS and coral through 2026, with and without recorded culling. Initial projections to 2050 link diver effort to removals, but peak sizes, recent densities and outside larval supply remain uncertain. Program-impact and fifth-wave suppression estimates still require independent validation.

**What was delivered**

- A 2027 priority ranking of all `r int(n_sites)` designated cull sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs (classes A–D; CSV and KMZ).
- `r int(nrow(expl))` exploration areas on `r int(length(unique(expl$reef_name)))` reefs: high-ranked habitat outside the cull sites and away from recent tows.
- 30 m habitat layers for the Great Barrier Reef, a known-aggregation-sites layer, and a pipeline re-run each season.
- The COTSMod.jl model, integrated with ADRIA, with a reproducible calibration workflow for the Lizard Island cluster.

**What managers can do now**

- Use the 2027 ranking as a search order. Agree and test the tolerance for missed >0.04 dives before adopting a fixed exclusion rule.
- Thin manta surveillance evenly if effort must be cut, and add tows where habitat ranks highest.
- Add one or two exploration areas per reef visit and log the outcome.

**Main limitations.** On reefs with no recent visits the ranking relies on habitat and is close to chance. Rankings learned from past effort partly encode crew behaviour, and densities at never-dived sites cannot be verified. The products have not yet been trialled in the field, and the metacommunity model has not passed its validation gates.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Background

## The management problem

Irruptions of crown-of-thorns starfish (*Acanthaster* cf. *solaris*; COTS) are a major cause of coral loss on the Great Barrier Reef [@death2012decline; @pratchett2017thirty]. The COTS Control Program suppresses irruptions by manual culling, which can protect coral when sustained at the right reefs [@matthews2024protecting]. A substantial portion of operational effort goes into searching for COTS, creating opportunities to improve where surveillance and culling are directed.

Manta tow surveillance records COTS and feeding scars and assesses reef irruption status. Crews then choose cull sites using manta results and previous culling records. The current EoTR register contains `r int(n_sites)` designated sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs, of which approximately 1,300 sites across 200 actioned reefs are typically culled each year [@gbrmpadashboard2026]. The dashboards bring together recent observations to support these decisions [@matthews2025intelligence]. In the held-out cull records from 2018 to 2026, `r p0(cs_ghost / cs_dives)` of dives found no COTS (ghost dives), and a further `r p0(cs_low / cs_dives)` found COTS at CPUE below 0.02 COTS per minute of bottom time (low-density dives).
<!-- Approximate annual site/reef activity supplied by the author in review 02,
with the COTS Dashboard as source. Confirm reporting period for the approximate
1,300-site figure before finalisation; register totals remain inline results. -->

The operational strategy links decisions from individual sites to voyages and regional priorities [@fletcher2020strategy]. In practice, tow routes mostly follow established cull sites around reef perimeters. Many sites were initially delineated from satellite maps in 2018, leaving gaps in lagoon bommie fields, shallow crests and isolated patches. Search can therefore repeatedly trigger dives where few COTS are found while overlooking other potential habitat. Reducing repeated searches in low-priority areas could free effort to search these gaps, improving both efficiency and the chance of finding previously undetected populations.
<!-- Current practice and the history of site delineation supplied by the author
in review 02; Fletcher supports the operational framework, not these specific
observations about the current site register. -->

Crews and GBRMPA analysts already hold useful information about recent culling, empty sites, and COTS or scars seen on manta tows. This knowledge is strongest on frequently visited reefs and within the established search footprint. Fine-scale habitat maps cover places with little recent evidence, including potential search areas outside that footprint, but say little about whether COTS are present this season. This project combines these sources to prioritise familiar sites and identify additional places to search.

## Earlier models this project builds on

Most COTS modelling has treated whole reefs as its spatial units, either across the GBR for regional planning [@condie2021interventions; @bozec2022cumulative; @matthews2020cotsmod] or on individual reefs to inform culling thresholds [@morello2014model; @plaganyi2020targets]. Reef-level species distribution models (SDMs), which relate species observations to environmental conditions, showed that larval connectivity and water quality explain much of the spatial distribution of irruptions [@matthews2020connectivity], and a hybrid machine-learning model estimates each reef's annual irruption probability [@stewart2026hybrid]. Population and ecosystem models help compare regional control strategies and ecological targets, but their whole-reef units do not identify where within a reef to search or cull.

Recent developments support finer spatial resolution. Coral species distribution models use satellite-derived multiscale terrain and benthic variables to map habitat for key coral taxa at tens of metres [@guillaume2025coral]. Their predictions and environmental predictors are inputs to the habitat modelling here, which maps COTS suitability at 30 m and combines it with recent program observations.

In parallel, advances in hydrodynamic and COTS larval-connectivity modelling provide a route to representing connections among smaller areas of reef. This project adapts COTSMod, a spatially explicit model of COTS populations and coral recovery [@matthews2020cotsmod], to represent site-level dynamics in the northern GBR irruption initiation box. It uses AIMS's high-throughput ADRIA ecosystem modelling framework and CoralBlox coral dynamics [@adriamethods2026; @dealmeida2026coralblox]. The prototype covers the Lizard Island cluster, with 2,895 sub-reef sites on 113 reefs. Its present transport inputs remain at reef scale; the fine-scale hydrodynamic network has not yet replaced them. This distinction matters when interpreting its capacity to represent within-reef differences (@sec-metacommunity).

## The decisions this work supports

The tactical work addresses two operational uses: reducing manta tow effort while retaining detection of COTS aggregations, and searching fewer cull sites while avoiding empty or low-density dives. For management, the priority is to retain dives above 0.04 COTS per minute of bottom time. Missing some dives between 0.02 and 0.04 is acceptable under the proposed operational decision criterion; these should not carry the same penalty as missed dives above 0.04. The 0.04 value is the management target used here, while ecological sustainability also depends on coral cover [@plaganyi2020targets; @gbrmpadashboard2026]. The existing retrospective analyses used ≥0.02 to define a problematic dive and <0.02 for a low-density dive. Those results are retained under their original definitions, alongside a separate evaluation of the unchanged rankings against the >0.04 management criterion (@sec-high-density).

Reducing search effort can miss COTS even when sites are dropped without a model. The evaluation therefore asks whether a ranking finds more aggregations or retains more high-density dives than random selection at the same effort. For manta surveillance, it also compares model selection with evenly spaced tows. These comparisons distinguish the value of the ranking from the saving achieved simply by searching less. Additional searches outside the familiar footprint address a separate question: whether effort released from repeat searches can improve coverage and detection elsewhere.

A strategic decision sits above these: how to allocate control among connected reefs in a cluster or region. When should culling stop on a heavily affected reef if its remaining coral cannot be protected? When should control continue on a reef whose COTS population cannot be brought below a local target, because reducing its larval export could protect other reefs? A site-level model of population growth, collapse, dispersal and coral consumption is needed to compare those consequences. Evidence of renewed population growth at Lizard Island [@chandler2023densities; @uthicke2024edna] also motivates assessing whether the emerging fifth primary irruption wave can be suppressed, and what resources this would require.

## Project objectives

The project addressed three objectives:

1. Develop GBR-wide predictive fine-scale habitat suitability models by connecting fine-scale COTS data to new high-resolution benthic and coral habitat data.
2. Optimise and standardise surveillance paths to improve irruption detection and operational efficiency, including a comparison against traditional perimeter-based surveillance.
3. Refine site-level management strategies for individual reefs through predicted suitable habitat and metapopulation modelling.

For Objectives 1 and 2, the report evaluates habitat layers, manta thinning and cull-site rankings combining habitat with recent evidence (@sec-cull). The 2027 product also identifies exploration areas outside designated sites and recent tow paths, so that search planning can extend beyond places already visited. Retrospective thinning tests the retention of observed aggregations; it does not establish the performance of new surveillance routes or exploration areas.

For Objective 3, the metacommunity prototype provides a platform to assess the effects of the culling program from 2012 to the present and compare future control strategies. The intended comparisons address stopping rules where local coral protection is no longer achievable, continued control of larval-source reefs despite limited local protection, and the allocation and additional resources needed to suppress the fifth primary irruption wave. Outcomes include COTS populations, larval export, and local and downstream coral loss and recovery. Historical culling is implemented as prescribed removals, and an initial effort-based model now supports exploratory projections. Independent validation and agreement on operational scenarios remain necessary before these comparisons can guide management (@sec-metacommunity-results). Methods describe the prototype and its calibration (@sec-metacommunity); Appendix E maps the Work Plan outputs to the report.

# Methods

## Observations and habitat information

The analyses combined records of where COTS had been found with maps describing reef habitat. The full cull archive covered 2002–2026. After excluding records with missing counts or invalid bottom time, records matched to designated cull sites covered `r int(crscope$matched_sites)` sites on `r int(crscope$matched_reefs)` reefs. Catch per unit effort (CPUE) was the number of COTS culled per minute of bottom time. The habitat models summarised cull outcomes for each site and year; search performance was tested against individual dives.

Two thresholds answered different questions. The original habitat models predicted cull CPUE ≥0.02. Empty or “ghost” dives found no COTS; low-density dives found COTS below 0.02. The management assessment focused on retaining dives above 0.04, the Control Program's adopted ecological target on reefs with less than 40% coral cover [@plaganyi2020targets; @gbrmpadashboard2026]. Dives from 0.02 to 0.04 inclusive were treated as intermediate: some could be omitted without the penalty assigned to missed dives above 0.04. The original model response was retained when assessing this management criterion.

Manta records supplied observations along tow paths. Strong evidence meant a COTS sighting, at least two counted feeding scars, or scars recorded as common in older surveys; records with neither COTS nor scars were negatives. The manta-based habitat models used `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "tows"))` labelled tows in `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "reef_years"))` combinations of reef and survey year (reef-years). Contributing monitoring streams included Control Program crews from 2016, the Reef Joint Field Management Program from 2012, and the AIMS Long-Term Monitoring Program from 1992. These are source-program periods; each analysis used its specified data subset.

Scooter-assisted large area diver-based (SALAD) surveys [@pratchett2022salad] and Reef Health and Impact Surveys (RHIS) [@beeden2014rhis] supplied additional COTS and coral observations for the multi-observation habitat model. ReefScan imagery [@bainbridge2024reefscan] supplied a separate check at recorded sightings, rather than training data for that model. Survey-effort tracks were unavailable for that check, so it could not estimate detection rates or absence. Appendix G describes the role of each source.

Habitat predictors described depth, seabed shape, wave exposure, turbidity and predicted habitat for three *Acropora* taxa [@guillaume2025coral]. They were assembled on a 30 m grid. ReefGuide supplied additional environmental layers [@reefguide2026]; their shallower coverage left gaps in some deeper reef areas, particularly beyond about 15–20 m. GBR10 bathymetry and geomorphic maps supplied further reef information [@gbrmpabathymetry2021; @gbrmpageomorphic2021; @roelfsema2021shallow]. Appendix B lists predictors and sources; Appendix G gives the fitting and mapping details.

## Models and their purposes

The habitat models asked whether environmental conditions could rank places within a reef. The search-ranking model then added recent observations to identify where crews should search first. These tasks differ from simulating how culling affects connected COTS populations and coral, which was the role of the metacommunity model. @tbl-model-purpose defines each model before its results are discussed.

| Model or comparison | Purpose | Information used |
|---|---|---|
| Annual full-extent habitat model, 13 predictors | Predict cull outcomes across the full habitat-map extent | Twelve terrain and coral-habitat predictors plus survey year; fitted to cull site-years |
| Annual limited-extent habitat model, 18 predictors | Test whether added environmental information improves the annual prediction | The same predictors and year, plus five ReefGuide layers; fitted to cull site-years |
| Manta habitat models | Rank tow locations with strong COTS evidence | The environmental predictors above, fitted to tow observations; versions with year and with differences among reef-years accounted for were compared |
| Recent-evidence site ranking | Set a search order for designated cull sites | Habitat rank plus the preceding season's cull dives and nearby manta tows |
| Multi-observation habitat model | Explain habitat associations while allowing for different observations | Cull, SALAD and RHIS evidence, terrain, geomorphic classes and coral habitat; implemented with a hierarchical model of species communities |
| Habitat updated by longer cull history | Test how much past finds add to a habitat forecast | Multi-observation habitat estimates and spatially weighted earlier cull records |
| COTS–coral metacommunity model | Simulate connected populations, coral consumption and responses to removals | Population and coral processes, larval supply, disturbance and historical culling in the Lizard Island cluster |

: Models and comparisons. Predictor counts for the two annual models include survey year. Original code labels and alternative combinations are mapped to these descriptions in Appendix G. {#tbl-model-purpose}

The search-planning map used the annual model with additional environmental information wherever its layers were available, and the full-extent model elsewhere. Scores were placed on a common scale before cells were ranked within each reef. The manta habitat models were tested as alternatives. The multi-observation model supplied ecological interpretation and uncertainty; it was not the operational search map.

The recent-evidence ranking combined habitat with last season's observations at or near each designated site, including whether a site had been searched without finding problematic densities. It therefore formalised information already used by crews as well as adding habitat information. Its performance must be interpreted in that operational context.

## Testing the search decisions

Predictions were compared among locations on the same reef in the same year, because those are the choices crews make. We withheld reefs or used earlier seasons to predict later ones, as set out in @tbl-evaluation-purpose. Comparisons kept effort or the share of high-density dives retained equal. Random selection provided a reference for the gains expected simply from searching fewer sites. Manta thinning was also compared with evenly spaced tows.

| Decision | How the prediction was tested | Comparison and outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Where habitat predicts COTS | Each reef was scored by models fitted without its group of reefs | Ability to rank observations on the same reef and in the same year |
| Which cull sites to search | All designated sites were ranked, including never-dived sites; recent evidence came only from earlier seasons | Habitat alone, recent evidence and their combination; sites searched and dive outcomes retained |
| Whether the ranking works in later seasons | The evidence model was fitted on seasons before each test season, 2019–2026 | The same search outcomes, evaluated season by season |
| Whether >0.04 dives are retained | Saved rankings were assessed at the higher threshold without refitting | Missed high-density dives, low-density and ghost dives avoided, and intermediate dives retained |
| Which manta tows to omit | Recorded surveys were thinned while keeping the same number of tows for each strategy | Habitat-ranked, random and evenly spaced tows; observed aggregations still detected |

: Evaluation of the tactical decisions. The season-by-season evidence model used earlier outcomes, but its habitat models were withheld by reef and were not also restricted to earlier years. {#tbl-evaluation-purpose}

An observed manta aggregation comprised at least two strong-evidence tows linked within 500 m in a survey. It was retained if any of its tows remained. Tow order was approximated from position around the reef because recorded sequence was unavailable. The test therefore assessed thinning of existing surveys, not new route design.

For the >0.04 comparison, “sites searched” counted the selected designated sites across the evaluated reef-years, including sites that had never been dived. The assessment asked what proportion of observed dives fell at those selected sites; it could not determine COTS densities at unvisited sites. We compared search effort at 80%, 90%, 95% and 99% retention of high-density dives and assessed intermediate dives separately. These retention levels explored the trade-off; none was an agreed definition of negligible omissions. Confidence intervals resampled whole reef-years, or whole surveys for aggregation detection, and repeated each comparison. Appendix H provides the full comparisons and uncertainty calculations.

## Seasonal products and field assessment

The 2027 product ranked every designated site using habitat and the latest 12 months of cull and manta observations, from June 2025 to May 2026. Sites were grouped into four priority classes. Additional exploration areas identified high-ranked habitat outside designated sites and recent tow paths. These were proposed places to search, not confirmed COTS aggregations.

A field trial will record sites searched, tows, dives, effort and COTS found, comparing the ranking with crews' normal planning. It will also count visits to exploration areas and later checks of deferred sites. Annual or pre-closure checks remain necessary: postponing a search does not necessarily reduce annual effort. Appendix G gives the product settings and proposed assessment design.

## Modelling water movement and larval connections among reefs {#sec-hydro-connectivity-methods}

**Hydrodynamic model and particle tracking.** [TO WRITE: Sev and Owen — describe development of the fine-scale Lizard Island hydrodynamic model, its spatial domain and resolution, environmental forcing and checks against observations. Explain how particles representing COTS larvae were released and tracked, including release dates and source locations, larval behaviour, mortality, competency and the treatment of particles crossing the model boundary. Identify the model versions, data sources and supporting references.]

**Connectivity matrices and network analysis.** [TO WRITE: Sev and Owen — explain how particle trajectories were consolidated into connections among sub-reef sites and reefs. Define the matrix entries, their direction and units, how release numbers and source reef area were accounted for, and the settlement and competency rules. Describe the network analyses used to assess exchange within reef groups, larval sources and the relative isolation of Ribbon Reefs, including comparisons with distance alone, variation among releases and checks for model-boundary effects. Distinguish completed analyses from planned tests and state which connections were supplied to the population model.]

The initial dispersal assessment used modelled daily mean larval concentrations at ages 5, 9 and 10 days for `r int(lc_scope$releases)` releases from December 2022 to January 2023. Concentrations were averaged by polygon area to sub-reef sites and then reefs, and ranked within each release before comparisons were combined. This assessed relative spatial patterns without letting differences in total larval load dominate. We examined how often each site ranked in the highest fifth at day 10, variation among releases, and cross-shelf patterns within latitude bands. These descriptive comparisons do not identify larval origins or settlement probabilities. Appendix K provides the supporting comparisons and their limits.

## Simulating connected COTS and coral populations {#sec-metacommunity}

The metacommunity prototype represents `r int(2895)` sub-reef sites on `r int(113)` reefs in the Lizard Island cluster. COTSMod supplies population growth, coral consumption, reproduction and larval dispersal; ADRIA supplies the domain, disturbance and scenario handling, coupled to CoralBlox coral dynamics [@matthews2020cotsmod; @cotsmodmethods2026; @adriamethods2026; @dealmeida2026coralblox]. Larval connections currently operate between whole reefs. Habitat and recorded removals vary among sites, but fine-scale water-flow connections have not yet replaced those inputs.

Historical simulations were compared with COTS and coral records from Lizard Island, Eyrie, MacGillivray and North Direction. The tests asked whether the model reproduced the timing and size of irruptions, low densities between waves, and coral change. Recorded culling was applied as removals, limited by the simulated animals available. A mismatch between available animals and recorded catches was treated as a model diagnostic.

The intended strategic assessments compare matched histories with and without culling from 2012 onward, then examine future stopping rules, control of larval-source reefs and resources for fifth-wave suppression. They must track local and downstream coral outcomes. The latest projections translate diver-hours into removals using a density-dependent catch rate, capped by the available adult population. They compare no further culling, recent effort, increased effort and reallocation among reefs under two climate pathways through 2050. These exploratory scenarios require independent validation and agreement on operational constraints. Appendix I documents the current calibration and projections; Appendix G retains detailed model methods. [TO CONFIRM: connectivity attribution, delivery of the fine-scale network, final model release and operational scenario settings.]

# Results

## GBR fine-scale habitat predictions {#sec-cull}

### Habitat layers: a consistent first ordering on every reef {.unnumbered}

The habitat layers provide a first search order across the GBR, including reefs with little recent evidence. Their absolute values vary with survey year and region (@fig-overview); within reefs, the cull-trained layers place their highest ranks along reef margins and outer slopes (@fig-maps).

![Within-reef habitat ranks on Eyrie, Batt, Broadhurst and Lady Musgrave reefs. Columns show the full-extent and limited-extent cull-trained models, the manta-trained model, the joint habitat model, habitat updated with cull history for 2027, and joint-model uncertainty (90% posterior interval width). The top 30% of each reef is emphasised. Satellite imagery: Esri World Imagery; full attribution is in Appendix H.](../outputs/figures/fig02b_four_reef_comparison_imagery.png){#fig-maps width="100%"}

On their own, the layers discriminate modestly between places on the same reef. On independent manta tows, the limited-extent habitat model reached a within reef-year AUC of `r ci3(mi("RG + year", "within_reef_year_auc"), mi("RG + year", "auc_low"), mi("RG + year", "auc_high"))` (@tbl-manta, @fig-manta). It placed `r p0(mi("RG + year", "top20_lift") - 1)` more strong-evidence tows in each reef's top-ranked 20% than chance. The manta model, trained on tows but scored leave-reef-out, reached `r ci3(mt("within", "auc"), mt("within", "auc", "low"), mt("within", "auc", "high"))` (Appendix H).

### Predicted habitat and recent evidence increase cull-site search efficiency {#sec-high-density}

Combining recent cull and manta observations with habitat improved search priorities and efficiency compared with habitat alone. This pattern held across seasons (Appendix H). The assessment compared sites selected by the rankings and the share of high-density dives (>0.04 CPUE) they retained. In the test over 2019–2026 (`r int(fw_dives)` dives in `r int(fw_ry)` reef-years), retaining 80% of those dives required searching `r hdci("sites_searched", 0.8)` of designated sites with habitat estimates plus recent observations; retaining 90% required `r hdci("sites_searched", 0.9)`. Both required fewer sites than habitat alone or random selection at the same retention (@tbl-search-highlights, @fig-high-density).

The combined ranking avoided `r p1(hd("low_avoided", 0.8))` of low-density cull dives (positive CPUE <0.02) and `r p1(hd("ghost_avoided", 0.8))` of ghost cull dives (0 CPUE) at 80% retention. At 90% retention it avoided `r p1(hd("low_avoided", 0.9))` and `r p1(hd("ghost_avoided", 0.9))`, respectively (@tbl-search-highlights).

Search reductions became smaller as retention increased. Retaining 95% required `r hdci("sites_searched")` of sites with the combined ranking, avoiding `r p1(hd("low_avoided"))` of low-density dives and `r p1(hd("ghost_avoided"))` of ghost dives. Retaining 99% required `r hdci("sites_searched", 0.99)` of sites and avoided only `r p1(hd("low_avoided", 0.99))` and `r p1(hd("ghost_avoided", 0.99))` of those dive classes, respectively.

The evaluation did not test whether annual full surveys or later checks would recover missed populations; proposed follow-up measures are discussed in @sec-monitoring.

Habitat alone separated locations with and without COTS only weakly. Its practical contribution was to cover places where recent observations were absent: `r p0(n_noev / nrow(pri))` of designated sites in the 2027 product were on reefs without dives or tows in the preceding 12 months. Those sites relied on habitat and should be treated as initial search priorities. Past observations carried most of the information on recently visited reefs, but also reflected where crews chose to work. Maps, habitat comparisons and tests beyond the familiar footprint are in Appendix H.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-search-highlights
#| tbl-cap: "Designated sites searched and low-density or ghost cull dives avoided at matched retention of dives above 0.04 CPUE, 2019–2026. All values are percentages; brackets give 95% reef-year bootstrap intervals. Low-density means positive CPUE below 0.02; ghost dives found no COTS. Intermediate dives (0.02–0.04 inclusive) are separate. Existing rankings were reassessed without refitting: habitat models were withheld by reef and the evidence model used earlier seasons. Follow-up surveys and annual effort are not included."
highlight_rows <- expand.grid(target = c(0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99), score = c("habitat", "combined", "random"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
highlight_rows <- highlight_rows[order(highlight_rows$target, highlight_rows$score), ]
highlight_metric <- function(metric) vapply(seq_len(nrow(highlight_rows)), function(i) {
  x <- highlight_rows[i, ]
  sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", 100 * hd(metric, x$target, x$score),
    100 * hd(metric, x$target, x$score, col = "low"), 100 * hd(metric, x$target, x$score, col = "high"))
}, character(1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `High-density retained (%)` = 100 * highlight_rows$target,
  Ranking = c(combined = "Habitat + recent observations", habitat = "Habitat alone", random = "Random selection")[highlight_rows$score],
  `Sites searched (%)` = highlight_metric("sites_searched"),
  `Low-density avoided (%)` = highlight_metric("low_avoided"),
  `Ghost dives avoided (%)` = highlight_metric("ghost_avoided"),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
```

![Retention of observed dives above 0.04 CPUE against actual designated site-years searched, using the existing forward evidence rankings. Random selection has the same site count on each reef. Shading shows 95% reef-year bootstrap intervals; dotted horizontal lines mark 80%, 90%, 95% and 99% retention. Habitat fits were held out by reef, while the evidence regression used earlier seasons. Follow-up surveys were not evaluated.](../outputs/figures/fig20_high_density_retention.png){#fig-high-density width=100%}

In the retrospective manta comparison, habitat-only selection did not outperform evenly spaced thinning. That comparison is an analytical benchmark; practical searches require crew judgement and recent observations alongside habitat. Appendix H retains the surveillance comparisons.

## The 2027 products combine priorities with exploration

The delivered ranking covers `r int(n_sites)` designated sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs. Its map shows search priority and the recent evidence behind each site.

The product also identifies `r int(nrow(expl))` exploration areas on `r int(length(unique(expl$reef_name)))` reefs, outside designated sites and recent tow paths (@fig-2027). These allow operators to direct some effort toward overlooked habitat. Historical observations on new ground supported investigating such gaps, but the proposed exploration areas themselves have not been trialled. Their detection yield and the annual effort required for added searches and deferred-site checks remain to be estimated or measured.

![Batt Reef and Eyrie Reef: 2027 cull-site priority (A red to D grey), manta tows of the last five seasons (blue) and exploration areas (purple, numbered by rank) over satellite imagery. On these well-surveyed reefs the exploration areas are outer-edge pockets, reef ends and, at Eyrie, part of the northern back reef that no tow has crossed in five seasons.](../outputs/figures/fig17_search_2027_exploration.png){#fig-2027 width="100%"}

## Preliminary larval dispersal patterns vary across the reef cluster {#sec-hydro-connectivity-results}

The larval-concentration maps showed uneven exposure to simulated larvae across `r int(lc_scope$sites)` sub-reef sites on `r int(lc_scope$reefs)` reefs during the 2022–23 spawning season. Persistent day-10 hotspots were concentrated on mid-shelf reefs south of the Lizard Island group, including Williamson, Mackay and Osterlund (@fig-larval-hotspots). Reefs toward the northern end of the domain generally ranked lower.

The Lizard Island group was not a persistent concentration hotspot at the later larval ages examined. Some releases produced higher concentrations around Lizard earlier in development, but these peaks generally did not persist (Appendix K). This may partly reflect the domain boundary, which excludes larval sources on reefs outside the model.

Cross-shelf patterns differed along the domain. In its central part, later-age concentrations were generally higher on mid-shelf reefs than on Ribbon Reefs at similar latitudes; the southern Ribbon Reefs did not show the same deficit. The mid-shelf–Ribbon contrast qualitatively matches the irruption contrasts in the regional monitoring checks (Appendix I), while the one-season concentration result remains sensitive to the domain boundary.

Following this project, network analysis will examine when reefs in the initiation box exchange larvae within tightly connected groups, and when groups become relatively isolated. Combining these results with larval-concentration patterns could identify periods and locations favourable to irruption initiation or escalation and feed into an early-warning system. The planned work will compare these signals with long-term monitoring and reef-level irruption estimates [@stewart2026hybrid]. Appendix K describes the network tests needed to assess this use.

![Persistence of simulated larval-concentration hotspots at day 10, across the model domain (A) and around Lizard Island (B). Colour shows the proportion of releases in which a sub-reef site ranked in the highest fifth of concentration within that release. The dashed box marks the enlarged area; grey shows land. This reformats concentration figure lc2 from the project analysis. High concentration does not by itself establish local retention, source strength or settlement.](../outputs/figures/fig28_larval_hotspot_persistence.png){#fig-larval-hotspots width="100%"}

## Historical COTS and coral dynamics provide a basis for testing control strategies {#sec-metacommunity-results}

The updated metacommunity model reproduced the broad sequence of historical irruption waves and coral decline and recovery on the four calibration reefs (@fig-metacommunity-cots-coral). The comparison used `r int(mcn("base_seeds"))` random-seed pairs, with additional parameter tests giving `r int(mcn("calibration_arms_per_cull_state"))` runs each with and without recorded culling. Lizard Island's first (1990s) COTS peak remains too small, and coral trajectories differed from the surveys in some periods. Manta and photo-transect coral estimates also differed because they sampled different parts of the reef.

The model represents the build-up of the fifth primary irruption wave, but exceeds observed densities on several reefs. This overshoot could understate the relative effect of contemporary culling, a sensitivity that requires testing. The paired culling trajectories demonstrate the model's response to recorded removals; they do not yet provide an independently validated estimate of the program's impact since 2012.

Exploratory projections compare continued, increased and reallocated diver effort through 2050 to demonstrate the new modelling capability. Increased effort reduced the simulated near-term COTS peaks, but coral gains varied with reef and climate pathway. These scenarios demonstrate the comparisons the model can support; they are not forecasts of likely outcomes. Appendix I presents the scenarios alongside recent-density and additional-reef checks.

![Historical COTS and coral dynamics on the calibration reefs, combining source Figures 1 and 4 from the 21 October snapshot. Left: manta-tow equivalents (dotted line: 0.22 COTS per tow). Right: hard coral cover, modelled relative to habitable area. Blue solid lines omit recorded culling; purple dashed lines apply it. Lines are five-seed means; darker bands span those seeds and lighter bands span all 65 parameter-test runs per culling state. These ranges are not confidence intervals. Black points show LTMP manta observations (coral bars: reported 95% intervals); orange diamonds show 9 m photo-transects. Survey supports differ. These are calibration and diagnostic comparisons.](../outputs/figures/fig22_metacommunity_cots_coral.png){#fig-metacommunity-cots-coral width="100%"}

# Implications for management

## Combining recent observations with habitat for daily searches

- **Combine habitat with recent observations.** Recent cull and manta evidence improved search priorities and retention of high-density dives. Habitat provides the first search order where observations are missing. Gains depend on the retention required; Appendix H gives the comparisons.
- **Direct effort toward overlooked habitat.** Maps and exploration areas give operators a consistent search order beyond familiar sites. The gains partly formalise crew knowledge; field trials must assess the proposed exploration areas. Appendix G details product design and Appendix H the supporting evidence.
- **Retain follow-up coverage.** Annual full surveys, pre-closure checks and new-evidence checks could find populations deferred by the ranking. Assess missed high-density dives, control delays and all follow-up effort before selecting stopping rules or claiming annual time savings. Appendix L sets out the design.

## Maintaining coverage during manta surveillance

- **Use habitat to guide additional searches.** Habitat-ranked tows did not outperform the evenly spaced thinning benchmark. Thinning recorded tows is not a practical field route; operators need spatial coverage, recent observations and local knowledge. Test added searches in habitats missed by perimeter routes. Appendix H gives the surveillance results and Appendix L explains their operational use.

## Assessing the culling program from 2012 to the present and beyond

- **Measure local and downstream benefits.** The metacommunity model provides a framework for comparing recorded culling since 2012 with the same history without control. Track COTS abundance, larval export and coral loss and recovery, while stating how outside larval supply is treated. Validation and the complete paired assessment remain necessary. Appendices G, I and L describe the design and current model status.

## Projecting suppression of the fifth primary irruption wave

- **Compare control strategies and resources.** Use the model to compare current effort, increased capacity, reallocation among larval-source reefs and starting or stopping rules. Report both local and downstream coral outcomes. The initial projections demonstrate this capability, rather than forecasting management benefits. Appendices I and L give the scenarios and development needs.
- **Develop an early-warning application.** Combine larval concentration with network analysis to identify when initiation-box reefs form connected groups that could favour irruption initiation or escalation. Test the signals against monitoring and reef-level irruption estimates before using them operationally. Appendix K sets out the proposed analysis.

## Monitoring operational performance {#sec-monitoring}

- **Trial the ranking with crews in January 2027.** Compare it with normal planning and assess the proposed 10–15% reductions in searches and low-density or empty dives. Agree the allowance for missed >0.04 dives and the maximum delay to checking deferred sites. Record initial and follow-up detections, exploration yield, annual coverage, travel and diver effort. Appendix L retains the field-trial design and author-completion items.

# Limitations

The search evaluation used outcomes from dives crews chose to make. It cannot establish densities at never-dived sites or the consequences of changing crew behaviour. Reefs without recent observations depend mainly on habitat, where discrimination is weak. Spatially held-out habitat scores reduce bias from scoring a reef with its own training data, but the season-by-season evidence test did not also restrict the habitat fits to preceding years. The evidence regression was tested forward in time; the entire combined modelling process was not a fully prospective forecast.

Spatial coverage also limits interpretation. The primary habitat layer joins models with different predictor coverage, and their rankings differ near that boundary. The explanatory joint habitat model relies heavily on fallback predictors in some regions. Values from the manta-trained model away from tow paths are extrapolations, including at some proposed exploration areas. The retrospective thinning result also depends on an inferred order around the reef, which may be less suitable for surveys that do not follow the perimeter. None of the proposed 2027 products has yet demonstrated its performance in a field trial.

The metacommunity results are calibration, diagnostic comparisons and exploratory projections within one northern reef cluster. Replicated runs and additional-reef checks improve the assessment but do not complete independent regional validation. Historical peak heights and between-irruption densities depend on the assumed relationship between manta observations and true abundance. Recent cull and SALAD observations helped construct corrected irruption inputs and also assess their fit. The current calibration uses five seed pairs and parameter sensitivity tests; projections additionally span five climate models. Those ranges do not capture all structural uncertainty. In particular, excess simulated COTS in 2026 carry into the near-term projections, outside larval supply is only approximately coupled to future coral, and thermal acclimation scenarios have not yet entered the reported ensemble. No estimate of historical program impact or future coral protection should be presented as validated until these assumptions and held-out performance have been assessed.

Larval connectivity has different roles in the two strands. It was not a predictor in the within-reef habitat ranking, whereas it carries population effects among reefs in the metacommunity model. The latter still uses reef-level transport and does not establish fine-scale transport among sites. Uncertainty in that transport, external larval pressure and coral disturbance must accompany any assessment of downstream control benefits.

# Recommendations and next steps

1. Agree the tolerance for missed dives above 0.04 CPUE, then trial the 2027 ranking with crews. Record site searches, tows, dive effort, intermediate and high-density outcomes, exploration visits and later coverage checks. The revised retrospective trade-off does not establish the proposed adoption targets.
2. Maintain representative surveillance coverage and trial habitat-guided searches beyond familiar routes. The retrospective thinning benchmark is not an operational route; Appendix H documents the comparison.
3. Trial a small number of exploration areas per reef visit and record outcomes, including nil results, so that the evidence base can expand beyond familiar sites.
4. Refresh the ranking each season and repeat its temporal evaluation as new observations arrive. Compare the product with current crew practice as well as a no-information baseline.
5. Complete expert review with GBRMPA, vessel crews and Traditional Owner operators, and agree ownership of monitoring and integration into Field Maps and the COTS Dashboards. [TO CONFIRM: participants, timing and operational owner.]
6. Obtain survey-effort information for additional observation sources, including ReefScan, to support independent assessment beyond places selected for cull dives.
7. Resolve the recent COTS population mismatch and complete independent validation of the metacommunity model before estimating the program's impact from 2012 to the present.
8. Extend the paired historical culling diagnostics to a complete program-impact assessment, reporting effects on COTS populations, larval export and coral trajectories, with the limits imposed by the external boundary stated explicitly.
9. Refine the exploratory fifth-wave projections under agreed effort budgets, climate conditions and starting and stopping rules. Test the recent population state and outside supply assumptions, and report domain-wide as well as local coral consequences.
10. Test finer-scale hydrodynamic connectivity against a distance-based control, and assess any coupling of search rankings to intervention scenarios before using it for management comparisons. [TO CONFIRM: link to Work Plan output F and the agreed pilot region.]

  Random = vapply(ms, function(m) p1(op(m, "random")), ""),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr")

## Appendix G: Detailed model specification and evaluation {.unnumbered}

The main Methods define each model by its purpose. This appendix retains the
implementation detail needed to reproduce it. Original software labels are used
in archived tables and figure legends; their meanings are mapped below.

| Original label | Description used in the main report |
|---|---|
| clean + year | Annual full-extent model (13 predictors) |
| RG + year | Annual limited-extent model (18 predictors) |
| manta / manta with year | Annual habitat model fitted to manta observations |
| manta within reef-year | Manta habitat model accounting for differences among reef-years |
| combined site ranking | Recent-evidence site ranking |
| HMSC joint | Multi-observation habitat model |
| HMSC + history | Habitat updated by longer cull history; distinct from the operational site ranking |


The habitat-model reporting follows the Overview, Data, Model, Assessment and Prediction (ODMAP) protocol for species distribution models [@zurell2020odmap]. This structure specifies the management question and prediction target, the observations and predictors used, the model fitting, how predictions are evaluated, and how the resulting maps should be used. The sections below describe these elements for the habitat and search-ranking analyses; the metacommunity methods describe the population model, calibration and prescribed culling separately.

### Data and response definitions {.unnumbered}

The COTS Control Program's full cull dataset covered 2002–2026 and supplied the site, date, number of COTS culled and bottom time for each dive. Records with missing counts or non-positive bottom time were excluded. Records matched to designated cull sites covered `r int(crscope$matched_sites)` sites on `r int(crscope$matched_reefs)` reefs; the wider cleaned dataset contained records from `r int(crscope$all_record_reefs)` reefs. The archived habitat fits used the full-period source dataset, while each validation applied its stated spatial and temporal subsets. [TO CONFIRM: data-access agreement.]
<!-- Full source-period coverage confirmed by the author in review 03, comment 41.
Matching details are retained in R/cull_sites.R and scripts 15–17, not repeated
in the narrative; numerical sample scope comes from script 23. -->

Two CPUE thresholds serve different purposes. The archived habitat fits and original validation defined a problematic dive as CPUE ≥0.02 COTS per minute of bottom time. A ghost dive found no COTS; a low-density dive found COTS at positive CPUE <0.02. This lower threshold identifies dives that might be avoided while retaining some control below the ecological management target. The revised management evaluation instead penalises missed dives above 0.04. Positive dives from 0.02 to 0.04 inclusive form an intermediate group: some can be deferred without the penalty assigned to missed >0.04 dives. Thus exactly 0.02 remains positive under the original response and belongs to the intermediate group in the new evaluation; exactly 0.04 also belongs to the intermediate group. Ecologically sustainable densities vary with coral cover, so 0.04 is the operational criterion for this assessment, rather than a universal coral-growth threshold [@plaganyi2020targets]. Habitat fits used a site-year response, while search selection was assessed against individual dive outcomes. The two thresholds do not change the definition of a manta aggregation.

The habitat model fitted to manta observations used `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "tows"))` labelled tows in `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "reef_years"))` reef-years, including `r int(mt("within", "auc", col = "strong_tows"))` with strong COTS evidence. Strong evidence meant a direct COTS sighting, at least two counted feeding scars, or scars recorded as “common” in legacy surveys. Strict negatives recorded neither COTS nor scars; weak single-scar records were excluded from model fitting. The observation archives included Control Program crews (2016 onward), the Reef Joint Field Management Program (2012 onward) and AIMS LTMP (1992 onward), as specified by the author. SALAD [@pratchett2022salad] and RHIS [@beeden2014rhis] observations contributed to the joint habitat model. ReefScan imagery [@bainbridge2024reefscan] supplied a separate presence-only check in script 10 and was not a fitted response in the delivered joint model.

Predictors were assembled on a 30 m grid in GDA2020 / MGA zone 55. The clean stack contained depth, slope, eastness, northness, bathymetric position index, vector ruggedness, sky-view factor, horizontal and vertical curvature, and three coral habitat-suitability surfaces for *Acropora* taxa [@guillaume2025coral]. Five ReefGuide layers added significant wave height, wave period, turbidity, bathymetry and slope. The joint model also used geomorphic classes and reef features. Appendix B lists predictor codes. Sources: @gbrmpabathymetry2021, @gbrmpageomorphic2021, @roelfsema2021shallow and @reefguide2026. ReefGuide coverage was reduced in some deeper areas, particularly beyond about 15–20 m. [TO CONFIRM: predictor product versions and resampling methods.]

### Habitat models and mapped layers {.unnumbered}

The clean + year model used gradient-boosted trees [XGBoost; @chen2016xgboost] to predict the problematic-density indicator from the clean stack and survey year. The RG + year model added the five ReefGuide predictors. These cull-trained models learned from locations selected by crews, often following manta evidence, so their scores reflect the program's sampling footprint as well as habitat. The operational refits used 1,500 boosting rounds, a learning rate of 0.00137382379588326, maximum tree depth 5, minimum child weight 20 and gamma $10^{-10}$, retaining the archived hyperparameters. These settings were not retuned on the evaluation reefs.

The primary search-planning layer used RG + year where available and clean + year elsewhere, calibrated onto the RG probability scale before combining them. Each 30 m cell was then ranked within its reef polygon, with map priority classes for the top 10%, 10–20% and 20–30%. RG + year covered `r p0(pick(lcov, layer_id = "legacy_rg_year2026", col = "fraction"))` of the reef-polygon support cells used in the coverage analysis. Of the mapped reefs, `r int(sum(rsrc$source == "RG only"))` used RG alone, `r int(sum(rsrc$source == "mixed"))` mixed the two sources and `r int(sum(rsrc$source == "clean fallback only"))` used the clean fallback alone.

Manta-trained XGBoost models used the RG stack and the same boosting settings. Predictor values were averaged along each tow. A model with survey year was compared with a model designed specifically to rank locations within reef-years. For the latter, the logit of the reef-year's strong-tow proportion, with a half-count correction, entered training as a fixed offset and survey year was omitted. The offset was omitted when predicting relative habitat scores because it was constant within a reef-year. The resulting map represents relative log-odds, not an annual occurrence probability. The cull-trained and manta-trained ranks were also compared as an average rank and as separate terms in the evidence model.

The hierarchical model of species communities [HMSC; @ovaskainen2017hmsc; @tikhonov2020hmsc] related cull, SALAD and RHIS responses jointly to habitat at 120 m, conditional on an active reef-year. Three predictor components supplied fallbacks where enhanced predictors were unavailable. Production fits used four chains, each retaining 1,000 samples at thinning 30 after 5,000 transient iterations. Convergence was assessed against a minimum effective sample size of 400 and maximum upper potential scale reduction factor of 1.1 (Appendix C). This model supplied explanatory habitat effects and uncertainty.

An additional layer represented known aggregation sites using a Gaussian kernel of the problematic rate in earlier active cull site-years (σ = 500 m). Its rate *H* and evidence weight *W* updated the HMSC habitat probability *p* as (κ*p* + *WH*)/(κ + *W*), with κ = 2 for the fixed-setting comparison. History and dive effort were interpreted as records of past finds and crew targeting, rather than independent habitat evidence.

### Evaluation design and search-efficiency analyses {.unnumbered}

Operational discrimination was measured among locations on the same reef in the same year. Within reef-year AUC compared positive and negative locations only within those groups; an AUC of 0.5 indicated no discrimination. Top-20% lift was the share of positives in the highest-ranked fifth divided by 0.2. These metrics were supplemented by the outcomes retained when effort was reduced.

For operational habitat comparisons, reefs were assigned to five folds and every reef was scored by a model refitted without any reefs in its fold [@roberts2017cv]. The pipeline calls this leave-reef-out validation; it is grouped five-fold validation, rather than one refit per reef. This prevented a reef's cull or manta observations from contributing to its habitat fit. A separate matched manta check scored the same `r int(mi("RG + year", "tows"))` tows in `r int(mi("RG + year", "reef_years"))` active reef-years on `r int(mi("RG + year", "reefs"))` reefs where all deployed layers were available. That check used the fitted layers and was not a substitute for the refitted operational evaluation.

Manta aggregations were connected groups of strong-evidence tow midpoints linked within 500 m in a survey (reef and date); successive links could join a group wider than 500 m. The principal aggregation analysis required at least two strong tows, with isolated records examined separately. Surveys required at least five scored tows and some strong evidence. An aggregation was retained if at least one of its tows was kept. This measured retention of observed aggregation evidence under retrospective thinning.

Each thinning strategy kept the same number of tows per survey, over retained shares from 90% to 30%. Model thinning kept the highest-scoring tows. Random thinning used the exact hypergeometric expectation of retaining at least one tow in each aggregation. Systematic thinning kept evenly spaced positions in the tow sequence, averaged over 20 starting offsets. Recorded tow order was unavailable, so sequence was approximated by bearing from the survey centre. The comparison therefore concerned thinning existing surveillance, not the performance of newly designed tow routes.

Cull-site analyses ranked every designated site on a reef, including never-dived sites, by its mean habitat score over the polygon. For each retained share of designated sites, the analysis recorded the share of observed problematic, low-density and ghost dives at retained sites. Random selection supplied a no-information expectation: retaining a fraction of sites gives that fraction's expected retention of each observed outcome. Outcomes at never-dived sites were unknown, so this exercise could not measure COTS missed at those sites or changes in crew behaviour under deployment.

To add recent evidence, each site received indicators for any problematic dive there in the previous season and for having been dived with none problematic. Neighbourhood terms were the problematic rate and dive effort among nearby cull dives, and strong-evidence and total manta tows, using a Gaussian kernel with σ = 300 m. Effort and tow counts entered logistic regressions after log(1 + *x*) transformation; missing habitat ranks were assigned the midpoint. Habitat alone, evidence alone, habitat + evidence and a simple flagged-sites-first rule were compared. The regressions were fitted on other reef folds, and evidence for a test year came only from preceding seasons. This spatial test did not also restrict regression training outcomes to years before the test year.

Rankings were compared at matched retention of problematic dives because evidence could move both problematic and low-density dives upwards. Retention curves were evaluated over 5% steps in designated sites searched and interpolated at 80%, 85%, 90% and 95% problematic-dive retention. The separate season-by-season test used 80% and 90%. For each test year from 2019 to 2026, its evidence regression was fitted only on earlier dive outcomes, comparing all earlier seasons with the last five or three, and cull-only, averaged cull–manta or separate habitat terms. Habitat covariates in this test were the reef-held-out ranks from the spatial analysis; the habitat fits themselves were not restricted to preceding years. Thus the evidence regression was tested forward in time, while the habitat component was held out spatially.

The >0.04 reassessment kept the saved rankings from the habitat-only, recent-evidence and manta-habitat comparisons and the season-by-season evidence test; none was refitted to the higher threshold. Dive counts and CPUE were rejoined to the saved scores using reef, year and designated site. For the forward test, the recovered dive counts and original outcome classes were checked against the saved evaluation sample, preventing repeated dives at one site from generating duplicated records. The candidate set remained every designated site on each evaluated reef, including never-dived sites. At each rank cutoff, effort was the actual number of designated site-years selected, summed across evaluated reef-years, divided by all candidate site-years. Consequently the proportion searched could differ slightly from the nominal cutoff on reefs with few sites or tied habitat ranks.

The reassessment reported retention and omission of >0.04 dives, low-density and ghost dives avoided, and intermediate dives retained. Random selection used the exact expected outcomes for the same number of sites on each reef; it matched the combined ranking's effort in the spatial comparison and all rankings' effort in the forward comparison. Curves were also interpolated at 80%, 90%, 95% and 99% retention of >0.04 dives, using the first crossing of each target over 5% rank-cutoff steps. This interpolation describes a trade-off between adjacent effort levels, rather than a validated stopping rule for an individual reef. Confidence intervals used 500 paired reef-year bootstrap draws for this reassessment, including the forward scores. Earlier ≥0.02 results retain their original calculations and bootstrap counts. The high-density reassessment retains the original spatial and temporal holdout limits of each ranking.

Site search counts describe candidate locations selected for a visit; tow effort, dive effort and annual coverage are separate quantities. A field trial will record tows and their duration, dives and bottom time, COTS outcomes, added exploration searches, departures from the proposed search order, and later checks of deferred sites. It will compare the ranking with crews' normal planning. Sites deferred on a visit will still be checked annually or before the reef closes to further control visits. Analyses of the full season must count those later checks and added exploration, so that shifting effort between sites or visits is distinguished from reducing total vessel and diver time. Existing records cannot estimate outcomes at unvisited sites or the yield of the proposed new routes.

The HMSC–history forecast used a separate temporal design: for each test year from 2022 to 2026, habitat models were refitted on earlier years and history used earlier active site-years only. First-visit cull site-years were compared within reef-years containing both outcomes, using habitat, prior dive effort, history and their blend. This distinguished habitat transfer from the persistence of previous finds.

Uncertainty intervals used paired bootstrap resamples of reef-years for tow and cull metrics, or surveys for aggregation retention. Operational spatial comparisons used 500 resamples; the season-by-season site-ranking test used 200. The same resampled units were used across scores to preserve paired comparisons.

### Seasonal products {.unnumbered}

For 2027, the selected cull-habitat + evidence model was fitted on `r int(src$training_dives[1])` dives from `r src$training_years[1]`. Recent evidence covered 1 June 2025 to 31 May 2026, the latest 12 months available, because calendar 2026 contained only January–May. Sites were ranked within reefs and assigned classes A (top 20%), B (20–50%), C (50–80%) and D (bottom 20%). The deployed habitat layer supplied scores for this product; the operational validation used refitted habitat scores.

Exploration areas were drawn from 30 m cells 0.5–16 m deep in the reef's top 30% of habitat, more than 100 m from designated cull sites and more than 150 m from manta tows in the preceding five seasons. Habitat was the mean of the primary-layer and manta-model percentiles, re-ranked within the reef, with the primary layer alone where manta scores were missing. Nearby pockets were joined, large patches split into compact areas of about 9 ha, and outlines smoothed and clipped to the reef outside cull sites. Areas smaller than 0.5 ha were removed; up to ten areas per reef polygon, at least 350 m apart, were retained. These areas identified places to explore beyond the recent search footprint.

### Metacommunity model and historical culling {.unnumbered}

The detailed calibration and spatial-kernel removal specification below records the 15 October setup. Appendix I describes the subsequent changes to settlement, coral settings, reef-wide removal allocation and effort-based projections used in the current Results.

The strategic modelling strand extended COTSMod [@matthews2020cotsmod] through the Julia package COTSMod.jl, coupled to ADRIA and the CoralBlox coral model [@cotsmodmethods2026; @adriamethods2026; @dealmeida2026coralblox]. COTSMod.jl supplied population transitions, coral predation and larval processes; ADRIA supplied the spatial domain, disturbance forcing and scenario execution. The prototype used the Lizard Island cluster, with 2,895 sub-reef sites on 113 reefs. Historical simulations beginning in 1991 were assessed against AIMS Long-Term Monitoring Program (LTMP) manta COTS and coral records on Lizard Island, Eyrie, MacGillivray and North Direction reefs. The model state was expressed as recruit, juvenile and adult densities per hectare of site area, with coral cover represented relative to habitable area.

Site-level habitable fractions came from benthic maps in domain v0.3 and its v0.4 extension. Historical heat stress was supplied through ADRIA, with cyclone exposure examined as an option. Reef-to-reef larval flows were divided evenly among sites within a receiving reef. Habitable fractions and prescribed removals varied among sites, but transport did not yet resolve within-reef flows. The 30 m habitat layers and evidence-based search rankings were candidate inputs for future coupling, rather than validated components of the metacommunity model. [TO CONFIRM: source and attribution of the annual 2018–2022 connectivity matrices, status and delivery date of Work Plan output F, and the planned coupling to the habitat layers.]

The working COTS formulation combined preferred-first per-capita grazing, survival linked to remembered preferred coral cover, adult senescence and preferred-food effects on reproductive condition. Larval production included a low-density Allee effect, juvenile survival included a saturating predator-pit term, and larvae were transported using reef-level connectivity and supplied from outside the domain. External supply was derived from the reef-level irruption-probability hindcast [@stewart2026hybrid]; its production multiplier was a calibration assumption, not measured recruitment. Mechanisms suggested by MICE, CoCoNet and ReefMod-GBR were examined as optional alternatives [@morello2014model; @plaganyi2020targets; @condie2021interventions; @bozec2022cumulative]. Testing a mechanism did not make it part of the working configuration. [TO CONFIRM: attribution and final choice of the annual connectivity matrices; the sub-reef hydrodynamic network had not replaced these reef-level inputs.]

Calibration used bounded comparisons of candidate mechanisms and parameter settings. Each screen was preregistered, included an exact-replay reference and recorded settings, seeds, input checksums and repository revisions. Candidate mechanisms had to pass a qualitative peak-and-trough gate before wider optimisation. Irruption peak presence, timing and height, inter-irruption troughs and coral trajectories were assessed together. Coral dynamics were also assessed with COTS grazing forced from observed records to separate coral-model errors from population-dynamics errors. Simulated adult density was converted to manta CPUE through an explicit observation model. The working linear conversion used *CPUE* = *qA*, with *A* in adults ha$^{-1}$ and *q* = 0.015 COTS tow$^{-1}$ per adult ha$^{-1}$; alternative scales and density-dependent detection, *CPUE* = *qA*²/(*A* + *A*½), were sensitivity analyses. These alternatives were kept distinct because they change both initial-density estimates and the comparison with observations. In-sample calibration and diagnostic screens were not treated as held-out validation or evidence of management benefit.

The replicated historical comparison used score v2, which scored North Direction against its raw series and omitted Eyrie's unobserved first wave from the peak count. Its three retained candidates were compared over five recorded seed pairs. The later v0.4 diagnostic extended forcing to 2026 and used score v3: the manta-based score on 1992–2021 plus 1.5 times a diver-anchored recent-density log error. Original and cull/SALAD-corrected irruption boundaries were crossed with earlier and revised coral thermal settings; exploratory chlorophyll-derived larval-survival modifiers were also screened. These later runs used one seed pair and prescribed culling was off. Their corrected boundary and recent-density score shared evidence, so the comparison was a diagnostic fit rather than a validation. The two score versions were reported separately.

Observed historical culling was included as prescribed removals. Cull records from the licensed CSIRO compilation were retained for reefs in the domain, grouped by site and year, and mapped to model sites on the same reef. Counts were distributed with weights proportional to site area × exp(−*d*²/(2σ²)) within 3σ of the cull-site centroid, normalised to preserve total counts. The primary width was σ = 210 m, with nearest-site allocation (σ = 0) and σ = 420 m as sensitivities; the nearest site was used if no centroid lay within the kernel. Allocated counts were divided by model-site area to obtain removals in COTS ha$^{-1}$. COTS below 15 cm were assigned to the juvenile stage and those at least 15 cm to adults, an explicit size-to-stage approximation.

September–December removals were assigned to the following LTMP reporting year and applied before spawning; January–August removals were applied after spawning in their reporting year. The annual implementation placed these removals immediately before or after the COTS predation and population-transition call. Requested removals were capped at the simulated juvenile or adult population present, recruits were left unchanged, and adult age and size substates were scaled by the surviving adult fraction. The model logged actual removals separately from requested removals, allowing a shortage of simulated COTS to be diagnosed rather than removing animals that were absent.

This culling implementation prescribed observed catches. It did not yet predict diver search, catchability, effort costs or adaptive starting and stopping decisions. The intended scenarios—primary irruption suppression, starting and stopping rules, and downstream consequences—require further calibration and independent validation before their management performance can be assessed.

#### Design of the historical and future control assessments {.unnumbered}

The intended historical assessment pairs simulations with recorded removals from 2012 onward and simulations without program removals, starting from the same pre-control population and coral state and using matching environmental sequences and random seeds. Outcomes will include actual removals, infeasible requested removals, COTS abundance, larval export, cumulative coral consumption and coral cover. Holding external larval supply identical estimates the effect of control within the model domain conditional on unchanged outside reefs. A regional no-culling assessment instead requires an external supply history consistent with no control outside the domain. This experiment is a planned extension of the prescribed-removal diagnostics reported here; no completed paired program-impact estimate is asserted.

Future comparisons will examine stopping when local coral protection is no longer achievable versus continuing to reduce larval export, and when to begin or intensify control on reefs whose COTS populations cannot be reduced below a local target. Reallocation within existing vessel capacity and additional capacity will be compared separately, using current control and no control as references. Feasible removals must follow population availability and an effort–catchability relationship, rather than prescribed catches alone. Each paired comparison will share climate, disturbance and random-seed sequences, and repeat across plausible population, coral, connectivity and observation assumptions. Local and downstream coral outcomes and the resources required for fifth-wave suppression will be reported together. [TO CONFIRM: final effort–catchability model, projection horizon, vessel budgets, intervention rules and climate scenarios agreed with partners.]
