### Recent evidence combined with habitat reduces the cull-site search {.unnumbered}

In the original ≥0.02 evaluation, ranking designated cull sites by last season's cull dives and manta tows, with the habitat layer ordering sites that lack recent evidence, reduced the search needed for the same problematic dives (@tbl-evidence, @fig-evidence). The ranking is a logistic model fitted on other reefs (leave-reef-out) that uses evidence from the previous season only, never from the season being searched. Held out over 2018–2026 (`r int(ev_dives)` dives in `r int(ev_ry)` reef-years), with 90% of problematic dives retained, the combined ranking:

- reduced the designated sites searched from `r p0(ev("sites_searched", 0.9, "habitat"))` to `r p0(ev("sites_searched", 0.9, "combined"))`;
- raised low-density dives avoided from `r p0(ev("low_dives_avoided", 0.9, "habitat"))` to `r p0(ev("low_dives_avoided", 0.9, "combined"))`;
- raised ghost dives avoided from `r p0(ev("ghost_dives_avoided", 0.9, "habitat"))` to `r p0(ev("ghost_dives_avoided", 0.9, "combined"))`.

All paired bootstrap intervals excluded zero. Gains were larger in recent seasons. In 2022–2026, keeping 80% of problematic dives needed `r p0(ev("sites_searched", 0.8, "combined", "2022-2026"))` of designated sites instead of `r p0(ev("sites_searched", 0.8, "habitat", "2022-2026"))`. Low-density dives avoided rose from `r p0(ev("low_dives_avoided", 0.8, "habitat", "2022-2026"))` to `r p0(ev("low_dives_avoided", 0.8, "combined", "2022-2026"))`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-evidence
#| tbl-cap: "Habitat-only ranking → habitat plus previous-season evidence, compared at matched retention of problematic dives (CPUE ≥0.02; held out). Brackets: 95% paired bootstrap interval of the difference, in percentage points."
cell <- function(metric, r, period) sprintf("%s → %s (%s)", p0(ev(metric, r, "habitat", period)), p0(ev(metric, r, "combined", period)),
  gpp(ev(metric, r, "combined", period, "gain_low"), ev(metric, r, "combined", period, "gain_high")))
rows <- expand.grid(r = c(0.9, 0.8), period = c("2018-2026", "2022-2026"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Period = sub("-", "–", rows$period),
  `Problematic dives kept` = p0(rows$r),
  `Designated sites searched` = mapply(cell, "sites_searched", rows$r, rows$period),
  `Low-density dives avoided` = mapply(cell, "low_dives_avoided", rows$r, rows$period),
  `Ghost dives avoided` = mapply(cell, "ghost_dives_avoided", rows$r, rows$period),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lllll")
```

![Habitat-only and evidence-informed rankings of designated cull sites compared at the same share of problematic dives retained (80–95%). Panels: share of designated sites searched (lower is better), and shares of low-density and ghost dives avoided. Evidence is from the previous season only. Bars are 95% bootstrap intervals over reef-years (2018–2026). Adding last season's evidence shifts every curve in the useful direction.](../outputs/figures/fig15_cull_search_area_evidence.png){#fig-evidence width="100%"}

The fitted model weighs the evidence in ways that match field experience:

- strong manta tows or problematic dives nearby raised a site's rank;
- a site dived the previous season with nothing problematic dropped sharply;
- a site that had itself been problematic ranked slightly lower than its neighbourhood suggested, consistent with culling having reduced it.

Most of the reduction came from ranking quiet and never-dived sites lower. Among dives actually made, discrimination between problematic and low-density dives rose only from `r a2(pick(eauc, window = "last_season", subset = "all", score = "habitat", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))` to `r a2(pick(eauc, window = "last_season", subset = "all", score = "combined", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))`.

A simple rule ("last season's flagged sites first, then habitat") searched the fewest sites but avoided fewer low-density dives than the fitted model. A three-season evidence window gave the same picture.

### The gain holds season by season {.unnumbered}

The evidence model was also tested using earlier seasons to predict later ones. Its habitat models were withheld by reef but were not restricted to earlier years. It avoided more low-density dives than habitat alone in every season from 2022, and searched fewer sites in every season from 2023 (@tbl-seasons). It did not help in 2019–2021, when fewer earlier seasons were available to learn from.

Pooled over 2019–2026 (`r int(fw_dives)` dives in `r int(fw_ry)` reef-years), with 90% of problematic dives retained, sites searched fell from `r p0(fw("habitat_only", "sites_searched_at_90"))` to `r p0(fw("cull_all", "sites_searched_at_90"))`. Low-density dives avoided rose from `r p0(fw("habitat_only", "low_dives_avoided_at_90"))` to `r p0(fw("cull_all", "low_dives_avoided_at_90"))`. Training on all earlier seasons matched the last five (`r p0(fw("cull_last5", "sites_searched_at_90"))` of sites) and outperformed the last three (`r p0(fw("cull_last3", "sites_searched_at_90"))`). Adding the manta model to the habitat term made no difference (`r p0(fw("ensemble_all", "sites_searched_at_90"))`), so the simpler cull-trained habitat term was kept.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-seasons
#| tbl-cap: "Year-by-year forward test of the cull-site ranking with 90% of problematic dives (CPUE ≥0.02) retained. Each season uses an evidence model fitted only on earlier seasons, with habitat models withheld by reef. Values are habitat alone → cull-trained habitat + last season's evidence (all earlier seasons)."
periods <- c(as.character(2019:2026), "2019-2026")
lab <- c(as.character(2019:2025), "2026 (Jan–May)", "2019–2026")
arrow <- function(p, metric, f = p0) sprintf("%s → %s", f(fw("habitat_only", metric, p)), f(fw("cull_all", metric, p)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Test season` = lab,
  Dives = vapply(periods, function(p) int(fw("cull_all", "sites_searched_at_90", p, "dives")), ""),
  `Sites searched` = vapply(periods, arrow, "", metric = "sites_searched_at_90"),
  `Low-density dives avoided` = vapply(periods, arrow, "", metric = "low_dives_avoided_at_90"),
  `AUC, problematic vs low-density` = vapply(periods, arrow, "", metric = "auc_problematic_vs_low", f = a2),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrlll")
```

A caveat applies to all cull-site results. A ranking is credited when it agrees with where crews chose to dive. Crews already use the previous season's knowledge, so part of the gain formalises current practice. COTS densities at designated sites that were never dived cannot be verified from these data.

### Retaining dives above 0.04 CPUE {.unnumbered}

Re-evaluating the unchanged rankings against dives above 0.04 CPUE showed how the acceptable omission rate constrains search reductions (@tbl-high-density, @fig-high-density). In the forward evidence test over 2019–2026, retaining 95% of these dives required searching `r hdci("sites_searched")` of designated site-years with the combined ranking, compared with `r hdci("sites_searched", score = "habitat")` using habitat alone and `r hdci("sites_searched", score = "random")` under random selection. The combined ranking avoided `r hdci("low_avoided")` of low-density dives and `r hdci("ghost_avoided")` of ghost dives at this retention. These are retained outcomes from observed dives; they do not establish the number of aggregations missed or the consequences of deferring unvisited sites.

The acceptable loss makes a large difference. Retaining 99% of >0.04 dives required `r hdci("sites_searched", 0.99)` of site-years with the combined ranking, leaving much less scope to avoid low-density and ghost dives. At the nominal top-85% rank cutoff, the forward ranking searched `r p1(pick(hdfixed, design = "forward", period = "2019-2026", score = "combined", nominal_fraction = 0.85, metric = "sites_searched", col = "value"))` of candidate site-years and missed `r cip(pick(hdfixed, design = "forward", period = "2019-2026", score = "combined", nominal_fraction = 0.85, metric = "high_missed", col = "value"), pick(hdfixed, design = "forward", period = "2019-2026", score = "combined", nominal_fraction = 0.85, metric = "high_missed", col = "low"), pick(hdfixed, design = "forward", period = "2019-2026", score = "combined", nominal_fraction = 0.85, metric = "high_missed", col = "high"), 1)` of >0.04 dives. The proposed 10–15% search reduction therefore cannot be assumed compatible with negligible omissions; the allowed omission rate must be agreed and tested in the field.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-high-density
#| tbl-cap: "Unchanged rankings evaluated at >0.04 CPUE. Percentage of designated site-years searched and low-density or ghost dives avoided at matched high-density retention; brackets are 95% paired reef-year bootstrap intervals. Low-density means positive CPUE <0.02. Spatial: 2018–2026; forward evidence test: 2019–2026."
hdrows <- expand.grid(design = c("spatial", "forward"), target = c(0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99), score = c("habitat", "combined"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
hval <- function(metric, i) {
  x <- hdrows[i, ]; period <- if (x$design == "spatial") "2018-2026" else "2019-2026"
  sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", 100 * hd(metric, x$target, x$score, x$design, period),
          100 * hd(metric, x$target, x$score, x$design, period, "low"),
          100 * hd(metric, x$target, x$score, x$design, period, "high"))
}
hdrows <- hdrows[order(hdrows$design, hdrows$target, hdrows$score), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(Test = hdrows$design, `Retention (%)` = 100 * hdrows$target,
  Ranking = ifelse(hdrows$score == "combined", "Habitat + evidence", "Habitat"),
  `Sites (%)` = vapply(seq_len(nrow(hdrows)), function(i) hval("sites_searched", i), character(1)),
  `Low avoided (%)` = vapply(seq_len(nrow(hdrows)), function(i) hval("low_avoided", i), character(1)),
  `Ghost avoided (%)` = vapply(seq_len(nrow(hdrows)), function(i) hval("ghost_avoided", i), character(1)), check.names = FALSE))
```

See @fig-high-density in the main Results.

Intermediate dives were tracked separately rather than treated as failed high-density detections. At 95% >0.04 retention, the forward combined ranking retained `r hdci("intermediate_retained")` of dives from 0.02 to 0.04 inclusive. Allowing their omission in the management criterion did not itself change the search order: the saved model still learned the original ≥0.02 response and recent crew observations. The spatial comparison and manta-habitat alternatives were likewise rescored without refitting. Full fixed-effort, matched-retention, paired-difference and per-season results are provided in `cull_high_density_*.csv`.

### Each source covers the other's gaps {.unnumbered}

#### Habitat layers: a consistent first ordering on every reef {.unnumbered}

The habitat layers cover every reef. They give a consistent ordering within each reef, which is useful wherever crews have little recent evidence. Across the GBR, each layer's absolute values mostly reflect survey year and region (@fig-overview). Within reefs, the cull-trained layers placed their highest ranks along reef margins and outer slopes (@fig-maps).

![The three main habitat layers across the Great Barrier Reef, shown as cell means at about 2.9 km. The two cull-trained layers (left, centre) are annual probabilities of a problematic cull site-year in 2026; the HMSC layer (right) is conditional on an active reef-year. Gaps in RG + year are reefs without ReefGuide layers, filled by the clean + year fallback in the primary search-planning layer.](../outputs/figures/fig01_gbr_overview.png){#fig-overview width="100%"}

See @fig-maps in the main habitat Results. Imagery attribution: Tiles © Esri — Source: Esri, i-cubed, USDA, USGS, AEX, GeoEye, Getmapping, Aerogrid, IGN, IGP, UPR-EGP, and the GIS User Community.

On their own, the layers discriminate modestly between places on the same reef. On independent manta tows, RG + year reached a within reef-year AUC of `r ci3(mi("RG + year", "within_reef_year_auc"), mi("RG + year", "auc_low"), mi("RG + year", "auc_high"))` (@tbl-manta, @fig-manta). It placed `r p0(mi("RG + year", "top20_lift") - 1)` more strong-evidence tows in each reef's top-ranked 20% than chance. The manta model, trained on tows but scored leave-reef-out, reached `r ci3(mt("within", "auc"), mt("within", "auc", "low"), mt("within", "auc", "high"))` (Appendix H).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-manta
#| tbl-cap: "Discrimination between strong-evidence and strictly negative manta tows within reef-years. Manta tows were not used to fit any of these layers. Lift is the share of strong-evidence tows in a reef-year's top 20% of tows, divided by 20%. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over reef-years."
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Layer = mic$layer,
  `Within reef-year AUC (95% CI)` = sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", a3(mic$within_reef_year_auc), a3(mic$auc_low), a3(mic$auc_high)),
  `Top-20% lift (95% CI)` = sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", a2(mic$top20_lift), a2(mic$lift_low), a2(mic$lift_high)),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lll")
```

![Independent manta tow check of the three habitat layers. Left: within reef-year AUC; right: top-20% lift. Bars are 95% bootstrap intervals over reef-years; dotted lines mark chance.](../outputs/figures/fig03_manta_independent_check.png){#fig-manta width="100%"}

The layers agree only in part on which cells rank highest. Median within-reef Spearman correlations were `r a2(pick(la, pair = "Clean + year vs RG + year", col = "median"))` between clean + year and RG + year, `r a2(pick(la, pair = "Clean + year vs HMSC joint", col = "median"))` between clean + year and HMSC, and `r a2(pick(la, pair = "RG + year vs HMSC joint", col = "median"))` between RG + year and HMSC (Appendix D). Where both cull-trained layers exist, the fallback and RG rankings correlate at `r a2(fbc$spearman)`, so ranks near the RG coverage boundary within a reef are less reliable.

#### Habitat alone as a cull-site ranking {.unnumbered}

Used alone to rank all designated sites on a reef, the held-out habitat layer retained problematic dives only slightly faster than low-density or ghost dives (@tbl-sites, @fig-sites). Searching the top 70% of sites retained `r cip(cs("problematic_dives_kept", 0.7), cs("problematic_dives_kept", 0.7, col = "low"), cs("problematic_dives_kept", 0.7, col = "high"))` of problematic dives. A ranking with no information would have retained `r p1(cs("dives_kept", 0.7))`, the share of all dives at those sites. Within reef-years, the AUC was `r a2(pick(csa, period = "2018-2026", score = "leave-reef-out", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))` for problematic versus low-density dives and `r a2(pick(csa, period = "2018-2026", score = "leave-reef-out", col = "auc_problematic_vs_ghost"))` versus ghost dives. The in-sample layer looked stronger (`r a2(pick(csa, period = "2018-2026", score = "deployed", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))` and `r a2(pick(csa, period = "2018-2026", score = "deployed", col = "auc_problematic_vs_ghost"))`) only because it had been trained on those dives.

Whether a site holding COTS is above or below the action threshold on a given visit depends mainly on irruption stage, earlier culling and the movement of aggregations. Recent evidence captures these; static habitat cannot. The habitat ranking does reach places crews have not tested: `r p0(pick(und, top30 = TRUE, col = "share_never_dived"))` of site-years ranked in a reef's top 30% were at sites that had never been dived.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sites
#| tbl-cap: "Diving only the top-ranked designated cull sites on each reef, held-out habitat ranking alone, 2018–2026. 'Dives kept' is what a ranking with no information would retain of every outcome. Brackets: 95% bootstrap interval over reef-years."
s <- c(0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Designated sites searched` = paste("top", p0(s)),
  `Dives kept (no-information baseline)` = vapply(s, function(x) p1(cs("dives_kept", x)), ""),
  `Problematic dives kept` = vapply(s, function(x) sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", p1(cs("problematic_dives_kept", x)), p1(cs("problematic_dives_kept", x, col = "low")), p1(cs("problematic_dives_kept", x, col = "high"))), ""),
  `Low-density dives avoided` = vapply(s, function(x) p1(cs("low_dives_avoided", x)), ""),
  `Ghost dives avoided` = vapply(s, function(x) p1(cs("ghost_dives_avoided", x)), ""),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lllll")
```

![Original ≥0.02 evaluation: share of cull dives that would still occur if only the highest-ranked designated cull sites on each reef were dived, ranked by habitat alone, by dive outcome. Left: held-out ranking; right: deployed layer (in-sample). The dashed diagonal is the share of sites dived. Bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over reef-years. Without recent evidence, problematic, low-density and ghost dives fall away at almost the same rate.](../outputs/figures/fig14_cull_search_area.png){#fig-sites width="100%"}

#### Cull history: strong where it exists {.unnumbered}

Problematic sites persist between seasons at a scale of about 0.5–1 km. In the strictly forward test, the blend of habitat and cull history reached a within reef-year AUC of `r ci3(fvh("combined_fixed"), fvh("combined_fixed", col = "auc_low"), fvh("combined_fixed", col = "auc_high"))`, against `r a3(fvh("habitat"))` for habitat alone (@tbl-forward, @fig-forward).

The forecast is strongest where history exists. It reached `r a3(fvh("combined_fixed", "with nearby history"))` with history nearby, `r a3(fvh("combined_fixed", "little or no nearby history"))` where history was sparse and `r a3(fvh("combined_fixed", "new sites"))` at sites never culled before. History lies within reach of only `r p1(hist$fraction_with_history)` of 120 m reef cells, so across most of the reef the blend falls back to habitat.

Part of the skill reflects operator behaviour: a score based only on how often crews had dived a site reached `r a3(fvh("effort"))`. This layer is therefore delivered as a map of **known aggregation sites** for briefing crews, not as habitat. Reef-context predictors at 0.5–1 km (windward position, distance to reef edge, channels, eReefs currents) did not improve habitat forecasts robustly (`r a3(fvh("habitat_context"))` vs `r a3(fvh("habitat"))`, overlapping intervals).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-forward
#| tbl-cap: "Forward validation: within reef-year AUC for problematic cull site-years, test years 2022–2026 pooled. Each score uses only data from before the test year. The deployed blend's 95% bootstrap interval over reef-years is given for all site-years."
meth <- c(habitat = "Habitat (HMSC refitted before test year)", habitat_context = "Habitat + reef context",
          effort = "Dive effort only", history_fixed = "History kernel", combined_fixed = "Habitat + history (deployed)")
subs <- c("all", "with nearby history", "little or no nearby history", "new sites")
tf <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(meth), function(m) {
  v <- vapply(subs, function(s) a3(fvh(m, s)), "")
  v[1] <- if (m == "combined_fixed") ci3(fvh(m), fvh(m, col = "auc_low"), fvh(m, col = "auc_high")) else v[1]
  data.frame(Score = meth[[m]], t(v), check.names = FALSE)
}))
names(tf)[-1] <- sprintf("%s (n = %s)", c("All site-years", "With nearby history", "Little or none", "New sites"),
                         vapply(subs, function(s) int(fvh("habitat", s, col = "site_years")), ""))
knitr::kable(tf, row.names = FALSE, align = "lllll")
```

![Forward validation of habitat, reef context and cull-history scores. Left: all test site-years with 95% bootstrap intervals over reef-years. Right: the same scores split by how much cull history lies within reach of the site. History carries the forecast where it exists; habitat carries it where history is absent.](../outputs/figures/fig09_forward_validation.png){#fig-forward width="100%"}

#### Where recent evidence is missing {.unnumbered}

Recent evidence is unevenly spread. `r p0(1 - pick(ecov, window = "last_season", col = "share_reef_any_prev"))` of reef-years were on reefs not visited the season before. On those reefs (`r int(nv_dives)` dives) every ranking was close to chance (AUC about `r a2(pick(eauc, window = "last_season", subset = "reef not visited", score = "combined", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))`), and habitat was the only information available.

Habitat also reaches ground that recent search has not covered. A tow was counted as *new ground* if no tow lay within 300 m in the previous five seasons. On new ground, the manta model ranked tows with a within reef-year AUC of `r ci3(pick(eng, ground = "new ground", score = "manta_within", metric = "auc", col = "value"), pick(eng, ground = "new ground", score = "manta_within", metric = "auc", col = "low"), pick(eng, ground = "new ground", score = "manta_within", metric = "auc", col = "high"))`, and the cull-trained layer at `r a2(pick(eng, ground = "new ground", score = "cull", metric = "auc", col = "value"))`. Strong evidence was more common on new ground than on repeat ground (`r p1(pick(eng, ground = "new ground", score = "cull", metric = "auc", col = "strong_share"))` vs `r p1(pick(eng, ground = "repeat ground", score = "cull", metric = "auc", col = "strong_share"))` of tows), partly because new ground is often surveyed early in an irruption. This is the basis for the exploration areas in the 2027 product.

### Manta surveillance: spread tows evenly, add where habitat ranks highest {.unnumbered}

**Systematic thinning found the most aggregations at every level of effort** (@tbl-thinning, @fig-aggregations-detail). With 60% of tows kept, it found `r p1(ag(0.6, "systematic"))` of the `r int(ag(0.6, "aggregations"))` aggregations of two or more strong-evidence tows in `r int(ag(0.6, "surveys"))` surveys. Random thinning found `r p1(ag(0.6, "random"))`, and thinning by the held-out cull-trained layer found `r cip(ag(0.6, "layer_cv"), ag(0.6, "layer_cv_low"), ag(0.6, "layer_cv_high"))`.

The largest cut that still found at least 95% of aggregations was:

- `r p0(mx("systematic_point"))` of tows for systematic thinning (`r p0(mx("systematic_assured"))` with bootstrap assurance);
- `r p0(mx("random_point"))` for random thinning;
- `r p0(mx("layer_cv_point"))` for thinning by habitat rank.

Results for 2022–2026 alone were the same: `r p0(mx("systematic_point", AGG_RECENT))`, `r p0(mx("random_point", AGG_RECENT))` and `r p0(mx("layer_cv_point", AGG_RECENT))`.

Ranking concentrates the kept tows in a few high-scoring stretches of reef, so aggregations in low-scoring stretches are missed entirely. Habitat rank is therefore not a good basis for dropping tows. It did find slightly more isolated single strong tows than random (`r p0(ag(0.6, "layer_cv", "isolated strong tows, all years"))` vs `r p0(ag(0.6, "random", "isolated strong tows, all years"))` at 60% kept). Scoring with the deployed (in-sample) layer instead of the held-out one overstated aggregations found by `r pp(ag(0.6, "layer_deployed") - ag(0.6, "layer_cv"))` percentage points at 60% kept.

Reef-level detection is robust to thinning whichever tows are kept. Irruption reef-years have many positive tows, so keeping about 60% of tows in 2022–2026 still flagged `r p0(op("Manta: outbreak reef-years still detected", "primary_layer"))` of irruption reef-years with the layer and `r p0(op("Manta: outbreak reef-years still detected", "random"))` at random (Appendix D).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-thinning
#| tbl-cap: "Share of COTS aggregations (two or more strong-evidence tows within 500 m) still found when manta tows are cut within each survey, all years. The layer is the cull-trained RG + year model scored leave-reef-out; the deployed column is the same layer scored in-sample. Brackets: 95% bootstrap interval over surveys."
k <- c(0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Tows kept` = p0(k),
  `Layer, held out` = sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", vapply(k, function(x) p1(ag(x, "layer_cv")), ""),
                              vapply(k, function(x) p1(ag(x, "layer_cv_low")), ""), vapply(k, function(x) p1(ag(x, "layer_cv_high")), "")),
  `Layer, deployed` = vapply(k, function(x) p1(ag(x, "layer_deployed")), ""),
  Random = vapply(k, function(x) p1(ag(x, "random")), ""),
  Systematic = vapply(k, function(x) p1(ag(x, "systematic")), ""),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lllll")
```

![Manta tows kept versus COTS aggregations found. Left: aggregations of two or more strong-evidence tows found as tows are cut, for the cull-trained layer (held out and deployed), random selection and systematic thinning; bands are 95% bootstrap intervals over surveys. Right: share found at 60% of tows kept, by aggregation size. Evenly spaced thinning loses the fewest aggregations.](../outputs/figures/fig13_manta_aggregation_cv.png){#fig-aggregations-detail width="100%"}

**A habitat model trained on manta tows is the best guide to where to add tows.** Manta tows provide about 20 times more training rows than cull site-years. The within reef-year manta model ranked held-out tows best (@tbl-mantamodel, @fig-manta-model). It found `r pp(pick(mra, strategy = "within_cv", keep = 0.6, col = "within_minus_cull"))` percentage points more aggregations than the cull-trained model at 60% kept (95% CI `r gpp(pick(mra, strategy = "within_cv", keep = 0.6, col = "within_minus_cull_low"), pick(mra, strategy = "within_cv", keep = 0.6, col = "within_minus_cull_high"))`). That is still below random (`r p1(pick(mra, strategy = "random", keep = 0.6, col = "found"))`) and systematic thinning (`r p1(pick(mra, strategy = "systematic", keep = 0.6, col = "found"))`), so its role is to direct extra tows rather than to remove them. Its top predictors were wave period and height, bathymetry and slope.

Training on manta did not improve cull-site selection. With survey year as a predictor, the manta model ranked cull dives at chance (AUC `r a2(pick(mrc, period = "2018-2026", score = "manta", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))`), because survey year took `r p0(year_gain_manta)` of its fitted gain. The within reef-year version matched the cull-trained model over 2018–2026 (`r a3(pick(mrc, period = "2018-2026", score = "within", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))` vs `r a3(pick(mrc, period = "2018-2026", score = "cull", col = "auc_problematic_vs_low"))`). Once last season's evidence was added, every habitat model gave the same result. Manta tows see COTS and scars from the surface along the reef perimeter, whereas a problematic dive measures how many COTS a diver finds in a site; the two are related but not the same.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mantamodel
#| tbl-cap: "Cull-trained and manta-trained habitat models on held-out manta tows (all three fitted on the same leave-reef-out folds). AUC: strong-evidence vs strictly negative tows within reef-years, with 95% bootstrap intervals. Aggregations: share found at 60% of tows kept."
mods <- c(cull = "Cull-trained", manta = "Manta-trained (with year)", within = "Manta-trained, within reef-year")
strat <- c(cull = "cull_cv", manta = "manta_cv", within = "within_cv")
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Model = unname(mods),
  `Tow AUC (95% CI)` = vapply(names(mods), function(m) sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", a3(mt(m, "auc")), a3(mt(m, "auc", "low")), a3(mt(m, "auc", "high"))), ""),
  `Top-20% lift` = vapply(names(mods), function(m) a2(mt(m, "lift")), ""),
  `Aggregations found, 60% kept` = vapply(names(mods), function(m) p1(pick(mra, strategy = strat[[m]], keep = 0.6, col = "found")), ""),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "llll")
```

![Cull-trained and manta-trained habitat models on both goals. Left: within reef-year AUC on held-out manta tows. Centre: aggregations found with 60% of tows kept, with random and systematic thinning for reference. Right: low-density cull dives avoided at 90% of problematic dives (CPUE ≥0.02) retained, for the habitat model alone and with last season's evidence. Bars are 95% bootstrap intervals. The manta model ranks tows best; for cull sites, last season's evidence brings every habitat model to the same result.](../outputs/figures/fig16_manta_response_model.png){#fig-manta-model width="100%"}

### The 2027 cull-site priority ranking and exploration areas {.unnumbered}

Every designated cull site (`r int(n_sites)` sites on `r int(n_reefs)` reefs) was ranked within its reef for the 2027 season, using the combined model with the most recent 12 months of evidence. The ranking is delivered as a CSV and as the EoTR cull-site KMZ, with each polygon coloured by priority class. Each polygon also carries its rank, its modelled chance of a problematic dive if dived, and last season's evidence. @tbl-classes shows what each class kept in the forward test.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-classes
#| tbl-cap: "Original ≥0.02 evaluation: 2027 priority classes and what searching through each class retained in the forward test (dives 2019–2026)."
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Searching through` = c("A", "A + B", "A + B + C", "All (incl. D)"),
  `Sites on the reef` = c("top 20%", "top 50%", "top 80%", "100%"),
  `Problematic dives kept` = p0(cls$problematic_dives_kept),
  `Low-density dives avoided` = p0(cls$low_dives_avoided),
  `Ghost dives avoided` = p0(cls$ghost_dives_avoided),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lllll")
```

The separate >0.04 class summary (@tbl-high-density-classes) makes the cost of stopping at a fixed class explicit. Searching through A + B + C retained `r p1(pick(hdclasses, nominal_fraction = 0.8, metric = "high_retained", col = "value"))` of observed >0.04 dives in the forward test; the remainder would have been omitted on those visits. These classes describe search order, not an established safe stopping point.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-high-density-classes
#| tbl-cap: "High-density outcomes for the unchanged class cutoffs, using the forward test of 2019–2026. Retained shares are percentages with 95% reef-year bootstrap intervals. Intermediate means 0.02–0.04 inclusive; high-density means >0.04. The fractions are rank cutoffs, not measured reductions in annual tow or dive effort."
class_fractions <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 1)
class_cell <- function(a, metric) {
  x <- hdclasses[hdclasses$nominal_fraction == a & hdclasses$metric == metric, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(x) == 1)
  sprintf("%.1f [%.1f–%.1f]", 100 * x$value, 100 * x$low, 100 * x$high)
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Searching through` = c("A", "A + B", "A + B + C", "All"),
  `Rank cutoff (%)` = 100 * class_fractions,
  `High-density retained (%)` = vapply(class_fractions, class_cell, character(1), metric = "high_retained"),
  `Intermediate retained (%)` = vapply(class_fractions, class_cell, character(1), metric = "intermediate_retained"),
  check.names = FALSE))
```

The two sources share the ranking:

- **Evidence ranks the top.** `r int(n_probev)` sites had a problematic dive last season and `r int(n_mantaev)` have strong manta evidence nearby.
- **Evidence also lowers sites.** `r int(n_quiet)` sites were dived last season with nothing problematic, which strongly lowers their rank.
- **Habitat ranks the rest.** `r int(n_noev)` sites (`r p0(n_noev / nrow(pri))`) are on reefs with no dives or tows in the last 12 months. Habitat alone orders them, as a first search order to update once manta tows come in.

The exploration layer adds high-ranked habitat outside the current search footprint (@fig-2027), so that the ranking does not keep consolidating search on the same places. It contains `r int(nrow(expl))` areas on `r int(length(unique(expl$reef_name)))` reefs, with a median size of `r num(median(expl$area_ha), 0)` ha, a median habitat percentile of `r a2(median(expl$habitat_percentile))`, and a median distance from a cull site of `r int(median(expl$nearest_cull_site_m))` m. On well-surveyed reefs such as Batt and Eyrie, cull sites and five seasons of tows already cover most high-ranked habitat. The larger opportunities are on reefs with little recent towing.

See @fig-2027 in the main Results.

## Appendix I: Updated metacommunity calibration and exploratory projections {.unnumbered}

This appendix reports the completed 21 October 2026 figure set for the current working model, identified in the source files as W-wave-lf04. The COTS and coral comparison combines source Figures 1 and 4 in @fig-metacommunity-cots-coral. The remaining figures appear below, with panels rearranged for portrait pages and the source summaries and uncertainty bands retained. Appendix J preserves the 15 October snapshot as a development record.

### Calibration updates and uncertainty {.unnumbered}

Since the earlier snapshot, the working model has incorporated revised coral thermal responses, a chlorophyll-based larval-survival modifier, wave-exposure effects on settlement, and revised initial population and coral settings. Initial fast-growing coral at Lizard Island was increased by 0.04 in absolute cover. Larger increases were rejected because they left too many COTS between irruptions. The linear observation conversion remains 0.015 COTS per tow per adult per hectare; nonlinear alternatives failed regional checks. These decisions improved the working calibration without identifying a unique population mechanism [@adriacalibrationreport2026].

The comparison comprises `r int(mcn("base_seeds"))` base seed pairs plus twelve one-at-a-time parameter perturbations of ±25%, giving `r int(mcn("calibration_arms_per_cull_state"))` runs in each culling state. Perturbations cover outside larval supply, background coral mortality, bleaching under low heat stress, the chlorophyll response, juvenile survival and initial fast-growing coral shares. Inner bands span the base seeds; outer bands span all runs. Neither is a probability interval, and joint parameter and structural uncertainty are not fully represented.

Recorded cull totals are now distributed among sites on the same reef in proportion to simulated population counts, retaining juvenile/adult stages and pre-/post-spawning timing. Removals remain limited by the animals available. This replaces the spatial-kernel allocation in the earlier diagnostic. Calibration scoring keeps culling off; paired culling-on runs provide the overlay. Earlier unmet-removal percentages therefore do not describe the current model.

### Recent densities and additional reefs {.unnumbered}

The recent-density comparison (@fig-metacommunity-recent-density) shows partial agreement with diver estimates and differences among reefs. Corrected external irruption probabilities and density targets share cull and SALAD evidence, so this is a diagnostic comparison. The additional reefs (@fig-metacommunity-additional) show the contrast between historical irruption reefs and low-density ribbon reefs, while individual peak timing and size remain imperfect. These checks do not complete regional validation; Ribbon No 10 has no LTMP series here.

![Recent adult COTS density with and without recorded culling, against SALAD diver estimates and catches converted to density (source Figure 2). The vertical axis is logarithmic. Lines are five-seed means; bands span seeds and parameter tests as in the main figure. Larval-input corrections and density targets share observations, so agreement is not independent validation.](../outputs/figures/fig23_metacommunity_recent_density.png){#fig-metacommunity-recent-density width="100%"}

![COTS trajectories on additional reefs outside the four-reef calibration fit (source Figure 3). Points show LTMP manta observations; Ribbon No 10 has no LTMP series. Blue and purple indicate culling-off and culling-on trajectories with the main figure's range definitions.](../outputs/figures/fig24_metacommunity_additional_reefs.png){#fig-metacommunity-additional width="100%"}

### Initial control projections to 2050 {.unnumbered}

The completed ensemble spans `r int(mcn("climate_models"))` climate models, five seed pairs, two climate pathways, nine culling levels and two treatments of the 2026 population state. The figures use the `r int(mcn("projection_arms"))` continuous-history runs without a population reset. Historical catches apply through 2026; effort-based culling begins in 2027. “Recent effort” uses 2023–25 diver-hours on each reef. Increased effort multiplies those hours; targeted effort reallocates the same total each half-year among reefs with at least 3 adults per hectare. Density-dependent catch rates determine adult removals, capped by the available population. Vessel travel and search costs are not represented explicitly.

Outside larval supply resamples historical irruption patterns and scales them by projected coral in the domain. These conditional scenarios include neither thermal acclimation nor external coral-larval supplementation. Excess simulated COTS in 2026 carry into the near-term projections. Proposed changes to the population reset, thermal acclimation scenarios and source-reef culling corrections had not yet entered the reported ensemble.

Increased effort lowered near-term COTS peaks, with climate-dependent coral outcomes (@fig-metacommunity-projection245, @fig-metacommunity-projection370). Reallocation could increase domain-wide removals without providing the largest benefit at the five displayed reefs (@fig-metacommunity-projection-effects). Population and coral summaries cover those reefs, whereas removals cover the whole domain. These summaries cannot establish domain-wide coral protection or an optimal allocation; local and downstream outcomes and operational constraints need further assessment.

![Exploratory COTS and coral projections under SSP2-4.5. Lines are medians across five climate models and five seed pairs. Bands show the 25th–75th percentiles for no further culling and three times recent effort, rather than confidence intervals. “Targeted ×1” reallocates the recent total effort. The dotted line separates history from projections. Recent population and outside-supply uncertainty carry forward.](../outputs/figures/fig25_metacommunity_projection_ssp245.png){#fig-metacommunity-projection245 width="100%"}

![The same exploratory effort comparisons under SSP3-7.0, with definitions matching the preceding figure. Lower COTS densities later in the period can accompany reduced coral food and should not be read as a control benefit.](../outputs/figures/fig26_metacommunity_projection_ssp370.png){#fig-metacommunity-projection370 width="100%"}

![Exploratory effort comparisons for 2027–2050. Points are medians; bars span the 10th–90th percentiles across climate models and seeds. The first three panels average Lizard Island, MacGillivray, North Direction, Eyrie and Martin; the last counts adult removals across the whole domain. “Recent” retains the recent allocation, “targeted” reallocates it, and multipliers scale total hours. These are model-conditional scenarios.](../outputs/figures/fig27_metacommunity_projection_effects.png){#fig-metacommunity-projection-effects width="100%"}

## Appendix J: Archived 15 October metacommunity comparisons {.unnumbered}

The candidate codes below are technical identifiers. W denotes the working
configuration; the version with more initial preferred coral at Lizard Island is
C3a; the version with lower background coral mortality is C6. They remain
calibration alternatives, not validated control policies. Methods and scenario
design are documented in Appendix G; the following results retain the frozen
15 October 2026 reporting snapshot.

### Metacommunity model: calibration and current limitations {.unnumbered}

#### Replicated candidates {.unnumbered}

The metacommunity model now reproduced both historical irruption waves on the reefs with two observed waves, although irruption heights and intervening densities remained imperfect (@fig-metacommunity). Three configurations were retained for further testing: the working configuration W, C3a with a higher initial preferred-coral share at Lizard Island, and C6 with lower chronic background coral mortality. Each was run with `r int(mc("W", "seeds"))` recorded pairs of ecological and connectivity seeds. Under the revised score v2, each candidate matched `r int(mc("W", "matched_peaks"))` of `r int(mc("W", "observed_peaks"))` observed historical peaks in every seed. Matching allowed a timing window; it did not establish accurate peak heights or performance on independent data.

The candidates retained different compromises (@tbl-metacommunity). Mean COTS losses overlapped in their variation across seeds. C3a produced a larger first Lizard irruption, `r msd(mc("C3a", "liz_peak_adults_1995_2000_mean"), mc("C3a", "liz_peak_adults_1995_2000_sd"), 1)` adults ha$^{-1}$, compared with `r msd(mc("W", "liz_peak_adults_1995_2000_mean"), mc("W", "liz_peak_adults_1995_2000_sd"), 1)` for W, and had a lower coral error. However, it left more COTS between irruptions. C6 reduced the troughs at the cost of a higher coral error, `r num(mc("C6", "coral_J_mean"), 3)` against `r num(mc("W", "coral_J_mean"), 3)` for W.

The qualitative gate was sensitive to the observation model. At *A*½ = 30 adults ha$^{-1}$, W passed in `r int(mc("W", "gate30_passes"))` of `r int(mc("W", "seeds"))` seeds, C6 in `r int(mc("C6", "gate30_passes"))` and C3a in `r int(mc("C3a", "gate30_passes"))`. At *A*½ = 10, W passed in `r int(mc("W", "gate10_passes"))` and C6 in `r int(mc("C6", "gate10_passes"))`. These are conditional calibration checks: the detection curve remains uncertain, and a passing qualitative gate does not replace held-out or regional validation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-metacommunity
#| tbl-cap: "Replicated metacommunity calibration on the four Lizard Island reefs (run 20261014T_48). Means ± SD across five recorded seed pairs; these are measures of stochastic variation, not confidence intervals. Lower COTS loss (score v2) and coral J indicate better calibration fit. Gate columns count seeds passing G2′ under the indicated density-dependent manta detection assumption, with A½ in adults per hectare. All candidates matched seven historical peaks in every seed at the linear observation mapping. No entry represents held-out validation."
mt <- mcs[match(c("W", "C3a", "C6"), mcs$candidate), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Candidate = mt$candidate,
  `COTS loss v2` = msd(mt$summed_loss_v2_mean, mt$summed_loss_v2_sd),
  `Coral J` = msd(mt$coral_J_mean, mt$coral_J_sd, 3),
  `Gate A½ = 10` = paste0(mt$gate10_passes, "/", mt$seeds),
  `Gate A½ = 30` = paste0(mt$gate30_passes, "/", mt$seeds),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lllll")
```

![Historical COTS trajectories for W, C3a and C6. Lines are means across five seed pairs and ribbons are one standard deviation across seeds; points are AIMS LTMP manta observations. Adult density is shown through the fixed linear conversion of 0.015 COTS per tow per adult ha$^{-1}$, and the dotted line marks 0.22 COTS per tow. Peak-height and trough mismatches remain despite successful historical peak matching.](../outputs/figures/fig18_metacommunity_candidates.png){#fig-metacommunity width="100%"}

#### Historical culling exposed missing populations {.unnumbered}

Prescribing the recorded historical removals exposed populations that were too small to support the observed catches. In the working configuration with the primary 210 m allocation kernel, `r p0(mcrv("Eyrie Reef", "unmet_share"))` of requested removals at Eyrie in 2021–24 could not be applied because the simulated juvenile or adult population was absent. Across the model domain, the corresponding share was `r p0(mcrv("domain", "unmet_share"))`. This discrepancy identified a failure to represent the recent build-up, rather than evidence that actual culling was ineffective.

Where simulated COTS were available, removals changed the historical trajectory. North Direction's simulated second-wave maximum fell from `r num(mcuv("nocull", "nd_second_wave_cpue"), 2)` to `r num(mcuv("cull210", "nd_second_wave_cpue"), 2)` COTS per tow. The summed calibration loss v2 increased from `r num(mcuv("nocull", "summed_loss_v2"), 2)` to `r num(mcuv("cull210", "summed_loss_v2"), 2)`. These single-seed comparisons tested the removal implementation and consistency with recorded catches. They did not estimate the benefit of a control policy, and culling was left off in the subsequent build-up diagnostics.

#### Extension to 2026 {.unnumbered}

The latest completed diagnostic runs extended the domain to 2026 and examined the recent build-up separately from the historical candidate comparison (@fig-metacommunity-2026). They crossed original and cull/SALAD-corrected irruption-boundary inputs with changes to coral thermal settings. With the earlier thermal settings and no chlorophyll modifier, correcting the boundary reduced score v3 from `r num(mcv("original"), 2)` to `r num(mcv("corrected"), 2)`. With revised thermal settings, losses were `r num(mcv("original", "revised thermal settings"), 2)` and `r num(mcv("corrected", "revised thermal settings"), 2)`, respectively. The revised settings removed the extra bleaching multiplier and raised the threshold below which bleaching mortality was reduced. The trajectories showed that both the food trajectory and boundary supply affected the timing and magnitude of the new irruption.

Exploratory chlorophyll-based larval-survival modifiers gave smaller additional changes: the lowest score v3 in the corrected-boundary screen was `r num(mcv("corrected", "revised thermal settings", "pb30"), 2)`, against `r num(mcv("corrected", "revised thermal settings"), 2)` with those modifiers off. Score v3 includes a diver-anchored recent-density error and is not numerically comparable with the earlier score v2. All of these extended runs used one seed pair. Cull and SALAD evidence contributed to both the corrected boundary and its assessment, so their apparent improvement was not independent validation.

![Single-seed extension to 2026 with original or corrected irruption-boundary inputs, under the earlier or revised coral thermal settings. Lines show adult density, with chlorophyll modifiers and culling off. Corrected boundary supply produces a larger late build-up; its response also depends on coral forcing. The same cull/SALAD evidence helped construct and assess the corrected boundary. These are diagnostic trajectories, without an uncertainty interval or an independent validation claim.](../outputs/figures/fig19_metacommunity_2026_diagnostic.png){#fig-metacommunity-2026 width="100%"}

No configuration has completed the full validation sequence. The model remains a platform for testing irruption mechanisms and developing control scenarios. Held-out reefs and years, regional transfer and sensitivity tests are still required before reporting benefits of primary-irruption suppression or rules for starting and stopping control. The fine-scale habitat rankings have not been validated as inputs to the metacommunity model.

## Appendix K: Preliminary larval-concentration comparisons {.unnumbered}

These comparisons support @sec-hydro-connectivity-results and reformat project figures lc4 and lc6. They describe concentrations, rather than source-to-destination exchange, at larval ages 5, 9 and 10 days across `r int(lc_scope$releases)` releases. The full source set, including concentration ranks, hotspot persistence, zone comparisons and the north–south profile, remains in `DataProcessing/connectivity_lizard/outputs/figures/`.

### Variation among releases {.unnumbered}

Concentrations around Lizard varied among release dates. Elevated early-age concentrations in some releases did not consistently persist to the later ages (@fig-larval-releases). Values compare the unweighted mean reef concentration within a zone with the mean across all reefs in the domain. They are relative to that release and larval age, rather than a fraction of larvae produced locally. The Lizard group comprised reefs within 20 km of Lizard Island after the outer-barrier and Ribbon classifications were applied. Full zone rules and the component tables are retained with the source analysis.

![Mean reef concentration in each shelf zone relative to the domain mean, by release and larval age. A value of one means the zone matched the domain mean for that release and age. Colours are clipped at one-eighth and eight times the domain mean; labels retain the source values, with values below 0.1 grouped. This reformats source figure lc4. The ratios do not identify larval origins or measure local retention.](../outputs/figures/fig29_larval_release_comparison.png){#fig-larval-releases width="100%"}

### Cross-shelf patterns and the domain boundary {.unnumbered}

The broad north–south gradient makes an overall Lizard-versus-other-reefs contrast difficult to interpret. Comparing cross-shelf positions within latitude bands gives a more useful view (@fig-larval-cross-shelf). The central Ribbon Reefs generally ranked below nearby mid-shelf reefs at the later ages, whereas the southern Ribbon Reefs did not show the same pattern. Latitude bands reduce the influence of the broad gradient but do not remove all spatial dependence or possible boundary effects.

These results describe one spawning season. The local analysis plan calls for source-to-destination matrices for individual releases, explicit checks of sources and losses at the model boundary, and comparisons against connections based on distance alone. Those tests are needed before attributing concentration patterns to retention within reef groups, interpreting Ribbon Reef isolation, or using the patterns to identify reefs for source control. Exploratory reef-label permutations in the source analysis did not account for spatial autocorrelation; their p-values are not used here as confirmatory evidence. This reformats source figure lc6. ## Appendix L: Management assessment and field-trial design {.unnumbered}

The main management implications summarise the five uses below. This appendix retains the detailed interpretation, scenario design and field-assessment requirements that support them.

### Combining recent observations with habitat for daily searches {.unnumbered}

The practical contribution of the search models is a consistent way to combine what crews have recently observed with habitat information covering places they have not visited. Recent cull dives and manta tows carry most of the information about the current irruption, while habitat provides a first search order where that evidence is absent. The resulting ranking reduced the designated sites searched for a matched share of problematic dives in the retrospective comparisons. Its value is therefore in helping crews decide where to look first and releasing effort to search habitat outside the established footprint. Whether this improves overall detection depends on what is found in the added searches, as well as which familiar sites can be deferred.

This use follows from the different information each source contains. Habitat describes the setting in which COTS occur, but it cannot identify the current population after recruitment, movement and earlier control. Conversely, recent observations are informative about the places crews have searched but leave large gaps. Combining them is useful even when habitat alone separates high- and low-priority locations only weakly. The combined score should be read as a relative search priority within a reef, with the evidence behind it available to planners.

The >0.04 evaluation shows a benefit from ranking sites, with its size depending on the retention required. At 80% and 90% retention, the combined ranking searched `r p1(hd("sites_searched", 0.8))` and `r p1(hd("sites_searched", 0.9))` of sites, respectively, compared with `r p1(hd("sites_searched", 0.8, score = "random"))` and `r p1(hd("sites_searched", 0.9, score = "random"))` at random (@tbl-search-highlights). Requiring 95% retention still reduced searches, whereas 99% required almost all sites. The smaller reductions at high retention should not be attributed to the change in CPUE threshold alone: earlier ≥0.02 examples used lower retention targets. Any operational choice must weigh the sites deferred against the high-density dives potentially missed.

One option for field assessment is to use the ranking for repeated targeted visits while retaining an annual full-coverage survey that includes all deferred designated sites. Positive manta observations, feeding scars or nearby high-density detections could trigger earlier checks, and a full coverage check before reef closure could provide another opportunity to find missed populations. These measures could reduce the time that false negatives remain undetected, but their recovery rate has not been measured. Their effort, detection limits and the ecological consequences of delayed control must be included when judging the overall benefit (@sec-monitoring).

The retrospective gains also include knowledge already held by experienced crews. Sites were selected for dives using previous observations and local experience, so the ranking partly formalises existing practice. A field trial is needed to establish how much it adds to crew planning, particularly at never-dived sites. Exploration areas provide a way to extend the evidence base: visiting a small number of them and recording nil results as well as detections would allow future rankings to learn from a broader sample of reef habitat. Historical tows on previously unsurveyed ground found strong evidence more often than repeat tows, but this does not establish the yield of the proposed exploration areas; irruption stage may contribute to that difference.

### Maintaining coverage during manta surveillance {.unnumbered}

The retrospective manta comparison provides a spatial-coverage benchmark for assessing search strategies; evenly spaced omissions are not a proposed field route. Model-based selection concentrated tows in a few highly ranked areas and could miss whole aggregations elsewhere. Even spacing retained better coverage of the observed aggregations. This finding concerns retrospective thinning of existing surveys: tow order was inferred from position around the reef, and new routes have not been trialled. Habitat remains useful for proposing where to add or repeat observations, subject to field assessment, especially beyond the current footprint. The surveillance objective therefore has two parts: preserve coverage when thinning familiar routes, and test additional searches in lagoon bommie fields, shallow crests and isolated patches that perimeter routes can overlook. The trial should account for effort used on both, so that shifting effort to new habitat is distinguished from reducing total surveillance.

### Assessing the culling program from 2012 to the present and beyond {.unnumbered}

The fine-scale metacommunity model was developed to reconstruct the third and fourth irruption waves and the emerging fifth wave in the initiation zone, assess how culling has changed COTS populations and coral trajectories since 2012, and guide future prioritisation. The historical assessment compares the observed program with a counterfactual in which the same reefs receive no control. Counts of COTS culled document the program's removals, but do not show how many animals would otherwise have survived, reproduced and dispersed larvae, or how much coral those animals and their descendants would have consumed. Linking these processes allows the model to assess effects extending beyond the treated sites.

We compared paired simulations beginning from the same population and coral state before control. One applied recorded removals from 2012 onward, focusing on the periods of control in 2014–15 and 2020–2026; the other omitted program removals. Both received the same heat stress, cyclone and other environmental forcing and used matched random seeds. Reproduction, larval dispersal and coral consumption evolved within each simulation. Differences in COTS abundance, larval export, cumulative coral consumption and coral cover provided the comparison of program effects within the model's assumptions. Requested removals exceeding the simulated population were recorded explicitly. [TO CONFIRM BEFORE FINALISATION: completion of the full paired historical assessment and removal-record coverage through 2026; this paragraph is drafted in past tense as requested.]

Matching historical peak timing alone is insufficient: the model must also represent irruption sizes, populations between irruptions and the recent build-up documented by divers. Initial population estimates, the relationship between manta observations and actual density, and coral recovery all contribute to uncertainty in the estimated effects of culling.

Larvae arriving from reefs outside the Lizard Island model domain also affect this comparison. Their supply is currently informed by the GBR-wide irruption predictions of @stewart2026hybrid. For a regional history without culling, we would ideally need corresponding predictions of what happened on those outside reefs without culling, so that their larval supply reflects the same counterfactual. The existing prediction layer does not by itself provide that causal comparison. Using the same outside supply in both simulations instead estimates the effect of culling inside the Lizard Island domain while holding conditions on outside reefs unchanged. Any estimate of coral protected must state which of these questions it answers.

### Projecting suppression of the fifth primary irruption wave {.unnumbered}

The forward-looking extension will assess how attempts to suppress the fifth primary irruption wave in the initiation box during 2020–2026, including increased resources during 2026–2028, could change subsequent irruptions and coral protection outcomes. Within the current domain, the first test is whether suppression reduces COTS densities and larval supply at its southern extent, including Irene Reef and Startle Reefs. Those results would help assess potential consequences farther south toward the Cairns region; a direct estimate of coral protection there would require a model domain or linked model that includes those reefs. This extension is partly developed and builds on the strategic questions addressed by earlier COTS population and reef ecosystem models [@matthews2020cotsmod; @morello2014model; @condie2021interventions; @bozec2022cumulative].
<!-- The control periods and increased-resource window are supplied in the
author's tracked edits in review 01; they are scenario context, not model results. -->

The scenario comparisons will focus on what increased effort from now can achieve in suppressing the primary irruption. This question differs from protecting coral at individual reefs after secondary irruptions are established, as discussed by @matthews2024protecting. One set of comparisons will reallocate existing capacity among reefs, for example by targeting dense populations on reefs that supply larvae to others. A second set will assess the additional benefit of one or two vessels. Comparisons within each capacity level will show the value of changing allocation, while comparisons across capacity levels will show what extra resources could achieve. Continuation of current control and no control will provide reference trajectories. Starting and stopping rules will be examined within this primary-suppression objective. A stopping rule based only on the inability to save local coral could abandon a reef that remains an important larval source. Scenarios should therefore compare stopping when local protection is no longer achievable with continued control to reduce downstream recruitment. They should also test when to begin or intensify control on source reefs whose populations cannot feasibly be reduced below the local ecological target. These comparisons will show whether downstream benefits justify effort that produces little immediate local coral protection.

Each paired comparison will use the same climate and disturbance sequences. Repeating it across plausible population states, biological processes, larval transport and future environmental conditions will help identify strategies that are robust to deep uncertainty in the system. The aim is to find strategies that continue to meet management objectives across a wide range of plausible futures, rather than selecting a strategy that performs best under one assumed future.

The outcomes will connect suppression to the duration and extent of high COTS densities, larvae exported to connected reefs, coral loss through feeding, and subsequent coral recovery. Fewer COTS at a treated reef need not produce a proportional local coral benefit, particularly if coral spared from feeding is later affected by heat stress or cyclones. Conversely, culling a large aggregation might not prevent substantial coral loss at that reef but could still reduce COTS recruitment and protect coral on connected reefs. The assessment therefore needs to follow both local and downstream consequences.

Future scenarios must also represent what crews can achieve. The initial projections now link diver effort and COTS density to achievable removals, alongside prescribed historical catches. That relationship still requires assessment against operational records, including search and travel costs, before starting and stopping rules can describe operational choices credibly. Site rankings from the species distribution models could help allocate searches, although that coupling has not been validated. Scenario design will depend on future funding and direct consultation with GBRMPA, program partners and contractors to reflect operational realities. The exploratory horizon is 2050 under SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0. [TO CONFIRM: vessel budgets, intervention rules and climate scenarios agreed with program partners.]

### Monitoring operational performance {.unnumbered}

A field trial of the 2027 site rankings from the species distribution models is planned for January 2027, while the strategic metacommunity model continues to be developed. Before each visit, the trial will record the recommended priority of each site. It will then record which sites crews searched by manta tow or dive, the effort used, the COTS found and any reasons for departing from the suggested order. Outcomes will be compared with the search order crews would normally use and with the modelled expectations in @tbl-classes. The original class expectations use ≥0.02 COTS per minute of bottom time. The separate >0.04 reassessment (@sec-high-density) supplies the more relevant high-density trade-offs, but neither retrospective test establishes what will be found in the trial or at unvisited sites.

The trial will aim for a 10–15% reduction in the number of designated sites requiring manta-tow searches on individual visits, with a negligible share of dives above 0.04 COTS per minute of bottom time missed. It will also aim for a 10–15% reduction in low-density or empty dives under the same allowance for missed dives above 0.04. Here, empty dives find no COTS, and low-density dives retain the report's definition of positive CPUE below 0.02. Dives from 0.02 to 0.04 will be reported separately: some may be deferred without the penalty assigned to missed dives above 0.04. These remain proposed adoption criteria: the retrospective reassessment does not establish both reductions at an agreed negligible omission rate. [TO CONFIRM: the numerical tolerance for missed dives above 0.04 and whether reductions are measured per visit or over the full season.]

A fallback option is an annual full-coverage surveillance round that includes every designated site, including those deferred by the ranking, using manta tows and follow-up dives as appropriate. A further coverage check before reef closure could catch populations that develop or remain undetected between visits. New COTS sightings, feeding scars or nearby high-density dives could prompt earlier checks of low-ranked sites. Crews should record coverage and reasons for revisiting, rather than treating a low rank as evidence that COTS are absent.

The trial should record >0.04 dives found during follow-up at deferred sites, the time since the initial visit, and the extra tow and dive effort required. Independent checks of a sample of deferred sites during the initial visit would help estimate the false-negative rate; annual detections alone could also include newly developed populations. A negative manta observation alone cannot establish that a site has no high-density population. Annual surveys and pre-closure checks offer opportunities to detect false negatives, without guaranteeing complete detection or coral protection during the delay. The 80% and 90% options therefore need assessment with an agreed maximum delay and omission allowance, rather than assuming later coverage makes their initial 20% or 10% omissions negligible.

Full-season effort must include annual full surveys, pre-closure and triggered checks, repeat dives and exploration visits. Sites deferred on one visit may be searched later, so the initial site reductions in @tbl-search-highlights cannot be read directly as annual time savings. Visits to exploration areas should be reported separately, with dates and irruption conditions recorded. If the trial meets the 10–15% improvement targets while remaining within the agreed missed-dive allowance and completing the coverage checks, the approach can be considered for adoption; otherwise, the ranking or search rules should be refined. [TO CONFIRM: trial design, monitoring owner and reporting route agreed with GBRMPA and vessel operators.]

Savings should be attributed to the ranking only to the extent that it improves retention of high-density dives at the same effort, or reduces effort at the same retention. Translating those gains into vessel time or money requires an agreed account of travel, search, diving and culling time. [TO CONFIRM: whether to estimate financial savings and which operational cost data to use.]

### Developing an early-warning system {.unnumbered}

The proposed application combines concentration patterns with release-specific network analysis to identify periods when reefs in the initiation box exchange larvae within tightly connected groups. Comparisons with distance-based connections and explicit checks of sources beyond the domain boundary are needed to distinguish hydrodynamic clustering from reef layout and boundary truncation. Repeating the analysis across seasons and comparing its signals with subsequent COTS observations and reef-level irruption estimates would assess warning lead time and false alarms. Appendix K describes the planned connectivity tests; no early-warning performance has yet been evaluated.
